items: Forms during high-temperature cooking. High doses caused cancer in laboratory animals. Those doses were much greater than the levels in food. All 29 restaurant french-fry samples in this table had acrylamide. The median of all 29 was 270 µg/kg, and the range was 117 to 1,030. Fuddruckers is not on this map. Its two samples were 346 and 452. A later FDA table, data through October 7, 2004, reports single samples: McDonald's french fries 428, Chick-fil-A waffle fries 271, Long John Silver's french fries 337, Burger King hash browns 768, Taco Bell Mexican pizza 53, and a Taco Bell bean burrito below the detection limit. Acrylamide forms when sugars and the amino acid asparagine are cooked at high temperature, as in frying. The FDA reports that high levels caused cancer in laboratory animals, and that those levels were much greater than the levels in human food. The map shows the chains in the 2002 fry table that are on this map. The marks are every tagged location, not the restaurants the FDA sampled.

Aggression and irritability These studies asked whether a food chemical is associated with aggression. Evidence that one chemical causes aggression in people is limited. A study of hyperactivity or irritability is not a study of aggression. None of these studies tested the restaurants drawn on the map. Of these, the trans fat study is the one that measured aggression in adults. The color and preservative studies are about hyperactivity, irritability, or attention. The soft-drink study counts fights and does not name a chemical.

Artificial food colors and sodium benzoate

McCann and coauthors, 2007, gave 153 children age 3 and 144 children age 8 or 9 a drink. The drink contained a mixture of artificial colors and sodium benzoate, or a placebo. Some mixtures were followed by higher hyperactivity scores. The Lancet. The outcome was hyperactivity, not aggression. Each drink mixed several additives, so the trial does not say which additive produced the change. The European Food Safety Authority later called the evidence limited. The effect was small, it was not consistent across ages and mixtures, and the authority did not change the safety evaluation of those additives. EFSA.

Dengate and Ruben, 2002, gave 27 children bread with calcium propionate or a placebo. The children had already been selected because their behavior improved on a diet that removed additives. Average behavior scores were not significantly different. Relative to placebo, behavior worsened for 52% and improved for 19%. PubMed. The group was small and already selected. The authors describe irritability, restlessness, inattention, and sleep disturbance in some children. The paper does not report a finding on aggression.

High doses in rats reduced litter size and the weight of the offspring. The highest amount was in chicken burritos: median 45.7 µg/kg, against 6.7 in hamburgers with toppings. It was not detected in cheese pizza, chicken nuggets, or plain patties. One Tex-Mex chain's foods had a median of 63.4 µg/kg. The other was below the detection limit. The paper does not say which chain was which. DEHA is an adipate, not a phthalate. In rats, a high dose reduced litter size and the weight of the offspring. The same reviews did not find the drop in testosterone seen with DEHP. The Tex-Mex chains in the study were Taco Bell and Chipotle.

Lower testosterone, lower sperm motility, and preterm birth. DEHP was in every hamburger with toppings. The hamburger median was 36 µg/kg. Chicken nuggets were 26, fries 23.7, chicken burritos 23, and plain patties 14. It was not detected in cheese pizza. Across all foods from one hamburger chain the median was 44 µg/kg, and from the other it was 23. The paper does not say which chain was higher. ATSDR reports that higher exposure in men has been linked with lower testosterone and lower sperm motility. Higher exposure in pregnancy has been linked with preterm birth and, in children, with a shift in the timing of puberty and with testicles that do not descend. In animals it damages the testes and, before birth, male reproductive development. The EPA review called the human evidence for those male reproductive effects robust. The hamburger chains in the study were McDonald's and Burger King.

Harm of the DEHP kind is not established. The highest amount was in chicken burritos: median 6,000 µg/kg in the 6 burritos tested for DEHT. Hamburgers with toppings were 2,200 µg/kg. None of the 3 orders of french fries had it. Cheese pizza, chicken nuggets, and plain patties were not tested for DEHT. DEHT is a terephthalate used in place of DEHP. In the animal studies the Consumer Product Safety Commission reviewed, it did not reduce fertility or sperm measures. The fast-food paper says most of those studies were paid for by industry, and that the few human studies of hormones do not agree. Harm of the kind shown for DEHP is not established. Those burritos were bought at Taco Bell and Chipotle. The paper does not say which of the two had more.

Linked with preterm birth. Evidence of male reproductive effects is slight. The only median above the detection limit was in plain hamburger patties: 16.5 µg/kg, and all 4 patties had it. DEP was also found in 5 of 10 orders of fries and 8 of 21 hamburgers with toppings, but those medians were below the detection limit. DEP is a weaker suppressor of testosterone than DEHP or DnBP in animal studies. The EPA review found slight evidence of male reproductive effects in people, and moderate evidence of a link with preterm birth. The patties came from the hamburger chains in the study, McDonald's and Burger King. The paper does not say which chain's patties were higher.

Can suppress testosterone in animals. Evidence in people is slight. DiBP was measured only in the first round. The highest median was in hamburgers with toppings: 2.7 µg/kg, in 7 of 8 hamburgers. Cheese pizza was 1.9 and fries were 1.2. Chicken nuggets and plain patties were below the detection limit. DiBP is close in structure to DnBP, and in animals it can suppress testosterone. The EPA review found only slight evidence in people. It said the studies were fewer, and the exposures lower, than for DnBP. The hamburger chains in the study were McDonald's and Burger King. The paper does not give a named-chain ranking for DiBP.

Higher liver and kidney weights in the parent animals. That study found no effect on reproduction. The only median above the detection limit was in plain hamburger patties: 16.3 µg/kg, in 2 of 4 patties. In hamburgers with toppings the median was below the detection limit, and the 95th percentile was 590 µg/kg. It was not detected in fries, chicken burritos, or cheese pizza. The paper found DINCH in hamburgers from only one of the two hamburger chains, and does not name that chain. DINCH is a replacement plasticizer. A two-generation study in rats found no effect on reproduction at doses up to 1,000 mg per kilogram of body weight a day. The parent animals had higher liver and kidney weights. The fast-food paper says later experiments disagree about the testes, and human studies are few. The hamburger chains in the study were McDonald's and Burger King.

Linked with lower testosterone and changes in semen measures. DiNP was measured only in the first round. It was in every chicken burrito, median 36 µg/kg. Cheese pizza was 5.9. It was not detected in hamburgers, fries, chicken nuggets, or plain patties. One Tex-Mex chain's median was 53 µg/kg and the other's was 11.5. The paper does not say which chain was higher. The EPA review found moderate evidence linking DiNP with lower testosterone and changes in semen measures. That evidence is weaker than the evidence for DEHP. The Tex-Mex chains in the study were Taco Bell and Chipotle.

Distribution centers Martin Brower publishes street addresses for distribution centers that supply McDonald's restaurants. Those addresses are geocoded and drawn with a factory mark. The list does not say where the food is manufactured, and it does not give the roads between a center and a restaurant. No line on this map is a delivery route.

Not detected. Not established as a testosterone suppressor. DMP was not detected in any of the 64 foods. DMP was not detected in any food in this study. It is a smaller phthalate, and it is not established as a testosterone suppressor the way DEHP is. There is no chain to rank, because the chemical was not found.

Can suppress testosterone. Linked with semen measures and a longer time to pregnancy. DnBP was in every hamburger with toppings and every cheese pizza. The medians were close: 4.8 µg/kg in hamburgers, 4.5 in fries, 4.1 in cheese pizza, 3.5 in chicken burritos, and 2.4 in chicken nuggets. The paper says the food medians were statistically similar. Across all foods from one hamburger chain the median was 5.0 µg/kg, and from the other it was 2.8. The paper does not say which chain was higher. DnBP can suppress testosterone. An EPA review of human studies found robust evidence linking it with semen measures and a longer time to pregnancy. In animals it disrupts development of the male reproductive system. The hamburger chains in the study were McDonald's and Burger King.

Animal studies report changes in the liver. DnOP was uncommon. It was detected in 3 of 8 cheese pizzas and 1 of 7 orders of chicken nuggets, and every median was below the detection limit. One pizza chain's foods had a median of 2.3 µg/kg. The other pizza chain was below the detection limit. The paper does not say which chain was which. DnOP was outside the EPA review of reproductive effects. Animal studies report changes in the liver. Evidence that it suppresses testosterone the way DEHP does is limited. The pizza chains in the study were Pizza Hut and Domino's.

A marker for PFAS in packaging, not a measurement of the food. Some PFAS are associated with cancer, developmental toxicity, and immunotoxicity. Of 407 packages, 33% had detectable total fluorine. Dessert and bread wrappers and Tex-Mex packaging had higher detection rates than the other food-contact papers. The main table does not name the chains. A subset of 20 packages was tested for individual PFAS. Some samples with high total fluorine did not show high levels of the PFAS that test could measure. The study measured total fluorine in packaging as a marker for PFAS, which are per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. The authors write that some PFAS have been associated with cancer, developmental toxicity, immunotoxicity, and other health effects. He says a party label must not control the attorney general. He says he would apply the same law and the same evidence standard to political allies and opponents, and seek an outside review when the office has a conflict. He says he would defend religious liberty, conscience, lawful self-defense, and other constitutional rights. He says he would focus prosecution on dangerous offenders while confronting trafficking, exploitation, and domestic violence.

South Carolina attorney general and Army National Guard colonel Alan Wilson's campaign says he joined the South Carolina National Guard after college, has served since 1996, and deployed during Operation Iraqi Freedom. It says he is the state's attorney general and is running for governor. He highlights child-predator prosecutions, a larger Internet Crimes Against Children task force, and the state's human-trafficking task force. He says he has gone to court against policies of the Obama and Biden administrations, including what he calls a transgender agenda. He says he backs President Trump on immigration enforcement and election integrity.

Retired Air Force lieutenant colonel and former federal agent. Her campaign says she served 21 years in the Air Force and worked as a federal supervisory special agent on terror networks, spies, and child predators. She says she directed more than 180 agents across eight countries and is the Democratic nominee for Senate. She says she takes no corporate PAC money. She says she backs I-194, which she calls The Montana Plan, to end dark money in Montana. She says her public answers on issues are posted so voters can compare them with the other candidates.

Combat veteran running for Congress. Alex Mealer's campaign says she is a West Point graduate who led soldiers as an Army bomb-disposal officer in Afghanistan, then earned Harvard law and business degrees. It says she worked in Houston energy finance, owns a small business, and is raising children in the area. She says she would ban members of Congress from trading individual stocks, seek term limits, cut taxes and regulations, and lower the cost of living. She says she would keep boys out of girls' sports and locker rooms, secure the border, and back law enforcement. She says she would push flood projects around Lake Houston and expand oil and gas so energy stays affordable.

Houston Republican running for Congress. Alexander Hale's campaign says he is a devout Christian and fourth-generation Houstonian who attended Baylor on a full academic scholarship. It says he studied finance, political science, philosophy, and business, and interned in Washington before running for the 7th District. He says he would champion Houston energy companies rather than subsidize competitors, and go after housing, insurance, health-care, and electricity costs Washington controls. He says Houston's crime rate needs federal help for local police, and that he would cut spending he calls wasteful. He says state and local governments should handle problems they understand better than federal agencies.

Candidate for secretary of state Alexander Kolodin is running for Arizona secretary of state. His campaign says accountability in that office starts with securing elections and reporting results voters can trust. He says he will harden election systems against manipulation, error, and interference so every legal vote is counted accurately. He says he will run elections that reflect voters' choices without bureaucratic overreach or partisan interference. He says he will modernize administration so results come faster without giving up accuracy, and he promises more transparency.
District 14 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

U.S. representative for New York's 14th District. Her campaign says she was born in the Bronx to a small-business owner and a mother who cleaned homes after moving from Puerto Rico, later worked restaurant shifts while her family faced medical bills, and won the seat in 2018. It says she was the youngest woman ever elected to Congress at the time. She calls for Medicare for All so health care is not tied to a job and so the government can bargain down drug and medical prices. She says housing should be treated as a right, with more affordable and public housing and protections for current tenants. She supports a Green New Deal built around clean-energy jobs, and she says undocumented immigrants should have a path to full membership in the country and that ICE should be abolished.

Incumbent · also running for mayor of Chicago He has filed for Chicago’s next mayoral race while seeking this second term. He told Capitol News Illinois he is focused on the job in front of him. Critics say a win in Chicago would mean leaving this office months into the term. Cites appointments, kiosks, a Chicago Real ID supercenter, and more services online so a license stop is not a lost workday. Backed digital driver’s licenses, limits on state grants to libraries that ban books, and rules for e-bikes and e-scooters. Second term: finish that work. He has also said license-plate-reader companies should not hand data to police to track immigrants or people seeking abortion care.

District 24 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

Army veteran running for Congress in New York's 24th District. Her campaign says she grew up in Houghton, enlisted before she could vote, and served at Bagram Airfield helping oversee flights in Afghanistan. It says she later taught, worked at the Department of Veterans Affairs until she was laid off during the DOGE cuts, and then decided to run. She says she would protect and expand Medicaid, arguing a Republican budget bill would cut coverage in the district and close rural hospitals. She says she would expand child care, home-repair help, and the low-income housing tax credit, and seek funding for rural buses and water systems. She says she would pass the PRO Act, defend abortion access and LGBTQ rights, and not be funded by large corporations.

Candidate for Ohio secretary of state. Her campaign says she is running because every voice matters and every vote counts. She says politicians in Columbus and Washington are trying to hold onto power, and that the power belongs with Ohioans. She says the secretary of state should protect each voter's voice and keep elections fair, secure, and accessible. She says voters should choose their politicians, and that she has fought officials who rig the system to protect their own power. She says she would restore trust in elections, protect personal data, and make government answerable on costs and the other problems families face.
District 12 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

U.S. representative and retired educator for North Carolina's 12th District. Her campaign says she has represented the Charlotte area since 2014 and organizes her work around health care, food, housing, and education, which she calls the 4 H's. She says she knows personally how hard it is to live without them. She says abortion is a private medical decision and that she is still fighting for equal pay and paid family leave. She says she champions public schools, teachers, and historically Black colleges, and she sponsored permanent federal funding for minority-serving institutions. She says Congress should restore the Voting Rights Act and stop what she calls an assault on the working class and the poor.

Candidate for Colorado secretary of state. Amanda Campbell describes herself as a Colorado native, a married adoptive homeschooling mother, and a constitutionalist. She says she grew up around petition campaigns through her father's political work and wants the public to keep access to the laws that govern them. She says the state and federal constitutions bind politicians, and that the secretary of state should defend them by warning the legislature and going to court. She says voters have a right to use the initiative process without politicians interfering. She says business filings should be simpler, and that election security should be improved with each county as the state grows.

Jefferson County clerk and recorder running for secretary of state. Amanda Gonzalez says she is Jefferson County's clerk and recorder, an attorney, and the Democratic nominee for secretary of state. She says she previously led Colorado Common Cause and worked on voting rights and the state's independent redistricting commission. She says that as clerk she has worked to expand ballot access, improve election security, and run elections in one of the state's largest counties. She says the office should serve Colorado, not her own politics. She says she will work so every voice is heard, every vote is counted, and elections stay secure.

Democratic nominee for Florida's 2nd District Her campaign says she was born at a Navy hospital in San Diego, moved to Florida at age two, and was raised mainly in St. Petersburg. She studied economics, international affairs, emergency management, and public administration at Florida State, then spent about a decade as an operations director on U.S. government programs. She and her husband are raising their family in the Big Bend. She says she would lower the cost of groceries, housing, insurance, and medicine by taking on corporate price gouging and expanding affordable housing and health care. She says she wants a seat on the House Agriculture Committee, a strong Farm Bill, and full funding for nutrition programs in the district. She says she would ban members of Congress from trading individual stocks, support term limits, and get dark money out of politics.

Organizer and chief of campaigns at Color Of Change, running for Congress. She says her roots are in Georgia's 1st District, where she has served on the Savannah Black Heritage Festival Committee and local civic boards. She holds a B.A. in American Studies from the University of California, Berkeley, and she describes herself as a mom and as a full-time caregiver for her father, a veteran. She says she will fight to fund rural hospitals, expand mental health care, and protect Medicaid, and she supports national paid family and medical leave. She wants apprenticeship programs, the right to organize, and federal investments that reach port and other workers, plus housing and wages that let people who work in the district live there. She says she will push flood protection and preservation of the Okefenokee, restore voting access, defend LGBTQ+ rights and reproductive freedom, and treat gun violence as a public-health problem, including a ban on assault weapons.

Economist running for governor of Vermont. Her campaign says she was born and raised in rural Vermont and has spent her career helping governments build economies that work for people. She says strong communities are built by neighbors, not by distant institutions. She proposes free universal primary and preventive care, with a community doctor for every Vermonter. She wants permanently affordable housing paid for in part by taxes on private equity, second homes, and luxury estates, and she wants to ban AI data centers. She says the state should invest in local businesses, farmers, workers, and cooperatives so more wealth stays in Vermont.
Secretary of State · New Mexico · Democratic

Doña Ana County clerk running for secretary of state. Amanda López Askin says she is in her second term as clerk of Doña Ana County, grew up in Las Cruces, and previously worked as a family and mental health therapist. She says she is running to protect the right to vote and to keep elections safe, secure, and fair. She says the office should make campaign finance more transparent. She says she would give small businesses clearer, more stable dealings with the state.

Yakima County commissioner running for Congress. She says she came from a family rooted in faith, agriculture, and service, worked in banking, and has used county office to challenge COVID rules, secure water, and flag fraud. She says government should protect people and leave decisions with those closest to the consequences. She says she will stand with President Trump on the border, energy production, constitutional rights, and federal spending. Her stated priorities are faith, family, agriculture, public safety, and freedom for central Washington.

Registered nurse running for Congress The campaign says Amanda Pusczek is a registered nurse who has spent more than a decade on double shifts and disaster work, and that she is running because rural hospitals, public schools, and family farms in north Alabama have been squeezed. She says she is not a millionaire and will not take corporate PAC money. She says rural hospital closures and cuts to safety-net programs have left medical gaps, and she wants federal help to keep emergency rooms and maternity care open. She supports a $15 federal minimum wage, stronger union rights, and antitrust rules aimed at meatpacking and other concentrated industries. She wants family farmers protected from what she calls a poultry tournament system, plus a federal right to repair farm equipment.

Physician and U.S. representative running in a new district. Ami Bera's campaign says he is a physician first elected to Congress in 2012 after working as Sacramento County's chief medical officer and teaching at UC Davis. It says he is a first-generation American who attended California public schools through medical school and is running in the new 3rd Congressional District. He says every American should have affordable coverage, and he opposes turning Medicare into a voucher system. He says he would cut waste and fraud, strengthen the doctor-patient relationship, and invest in research including stem cell research. He says rural and mountain communities need primary care, telehealth, broadband, and stable funding for rural hospitals and clinics.

Emergency physician and former state representative running for Congress in Arizona's 1st District. His campaign says he is an emergency doctor who won three terms in the Arizona House and had more bills signed than any Democrat in the legislature over the last decade. He says that work focused on teacher pay, small businesses, and public health. He says he would roll back tariffs he calls a tax on groceries and gas, and protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid. He says only a woman and her doctor should make reproductive decisions, and he wants abortion rights written into federal law. He says he would reduce gun violence, fund police, stop fentanyl, and fight for Arizona's share of Colorado River water.

Educator and entrepreneur running for Congress The campaign says Ammie Akin is an educator and entrepreneur who has taught students with disabilities, trained school leaders, and with her husband is turning a former elementary school into a shared campus for nonprofits. She says she is ready to represent Alabama's 7th District. She says she will put families, workers, small businesses, and local communities ahead of party politics and will fight wasteful federal spending. She wants rural hospitals kept open and health care that does not depend on how far a family lives from a provider. She says schools should be a partnership among teachers, parents, and the community, and that students should be prepared for college or a career.

Physician running for governor. Her campaign says she grew up in Youngstown under difficult circumstances and is a doctor, advocate, and problem-solver. She says she is running because families are struggling while wealthy interests pull the state in another direction. The site lists lower household costs, health-care costs, education, jobs, worker protections, safer communities, and corruption as her priorities. A campaign update says medical debt should be eliminated and health care made more affordable. She also lists reproductive freedom and the ability to age in place among the issues on the site.

Physician running for Congress The campaign says Dr. Amy Chai is a primary-care and addiction physician running for Connecticut's 1st District. She describes growing up in extreme poverty, training at Johns Hopkins, Indiana University, Michigan, and Virginia, and later being named a U.S. Presidential Teacher. She says the middle class is struggling and that she wants local economies, small businesses, and American industry strengthened so people can afford a home and a family. Her issues page also focuses on health care, mental health and addiction, education and parents' rights, and taxes. She says government spending and legislation should be easier for the public to see.

U.S. senator and former Hennepin County attorney. Her campaign says she led Hennepin County's prosecutor's office for eight years and has served in the Senate, where she highlights bipartisan bills and a law letting Medicare negotiate drug prices. She is running for governor and says she wants state government to be more accountable. She says she would work to lower health care, housing, child care, and utility bills, and to build more homes. She says she would root out fraud and make it easier to start a business and get a permit. She says she would take on organized crime and gang violence and help local police hire and keep officers.
District 11 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Democratic

U.S. representative and former union organizer for New Jersey's 11th District. Her campaign says she is an Afro-Latina mother from New Jersey, the daughter of Colombian and Dominican immigrants, who watched her mother work as a seamstress until a union job changed the family's finances. She says she led New Jersey Working Families, directed politics for Bernie Sanders's 2020 campaign, and served in the Labor Department. She says she has spent 25 years fighting for working families, including New Jersey's $15 minimum wage and paid sick days. She says she is taking that fight to Washington and will take on bosses and bullies in both parties.

Attorney general of Massachusetts, running for re-election. Andrea Campbell's site says she was born and raised in Roxbury and the South End, went from foster care to Princeton and into public service, and is the first Black woman to serve as the state's attorney general. She says she is trying to make life more affordable by putting money back into people's pockets. She says she is defending freedoms against rollbacks from the Trump era. She says she is fighting for the next generation and for wider opportunity for every child, including reproductive rights, civil rights, and cases against powerful corporations.

Independent candidate for governor. Andrea James's site says her family has lived in Massachusetts for seven generations and that she is running to put the government's agenda on the needs of people. She says a governor's priorities should be housing, health care, child care, education, and quality of life, and she calls housing a human right. She says people should be able to see a doctor without going into debt and that families should have child care they trust. She says Massachusetts should not have contracts with ICE, and she wants data centers banned in favor of lower utility costs and green energy.

U.S. representative for Oregon's 6th District, seeking another term. Her campaign says her father immigrated from Mexico, served in the military, and spent three decades as a police officer, and that she was the first in her family to finish college. It says she worked in the Oregon Legislature on health care, the minimum wage, and paid family leave before her election to Congress. She says she will fight rising costs for working families, seek more living-wage jobs, and keep backing worker protections and investments in rural health care, education, and infrastructure. She says she led efforts to cap prescription prices in Oregon and is pushing Congress to let Medicare negotiate drug prices and to strengthen hospital and insurance price transparency. She also treats mental health and substance use as part of health care that is too often overlooked.

Health-care and business candidate running for Congress in Wisconsin's 5th District. His campaign says he is the son of Wisconsin's union movement, a product of public schools, and not a career politician. It says he built a career in health care and business beside workers and manufacturers. He says he would bring practical leadership aimed at lower costs, good-paying jobs, and better health care. He says protecting fair elections and democratic institutions is the issue that makes progress on jobs, health care, and education possible. He says women must be able to make their own reproductive-health decisions and that Congress should secure that right.

U.S. representative, Navy veteran, and firearms-business owner. He says he was commissioned from Notre Dame, served 28 years in the Navy including three combat deployments to Kuwait and Iraq, then earned a master's from the University of Georgia and built Clyde Armory from a garage hobby into a company with two Georgia stores. Elected in 2020, he says he serves on the Appropriations and Budget committees. He says that on April 12, 2013, the IRS confiscated $940,000 from his business through civil asset forfeiture, and that the agency later offered to return part of it if he forfeited the rest. He says most small-business owners hit by that process lacked the money to fight, and he presents the case as a fight against overreaching government. On guns, he argues that taxes on firearms and ammunition, from the National Firearms Act to local per-gun taxes, treat a constitutional right as a privilege and could tax it out of reach.
District 2 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

U.S. representative for New York's 2nd District. His campaign says he has represented the district since 2021 and chairs the House Homeland Security Committee. It also says he is vice chair of a Financial Services subcommittee on capital markets. He says he led the push for permanent funding of the World Trade Center Health Program. He says a tax law he supported raised the state-and-local tax deduction cap from $10,000 to $40,000 and ended federal tax on tips. He also points to an expanded child tax credit, a new deduction for seniors, and a policing bill he says passed the House.

Independent candidate for the U.S. Senate. He says he is a working-class candidate whose jobs have included military service, security, commercial trucking, information technology, food service, maintenance, and scientific research. He says he is running without political connections because he is tired of the status quo. He says government should keep life safe, affordable, peaceful, healthy, and fair, with personal liberty as the minimum. He says tax money should not go mainly to regime-change wars or to tax breaks for corporations that have not shown loyalty to the public. He says candidates, including himself, have a duty to serve the public rather than foreign governments or corporations.

Small-business owner and plumber running for Congress The campaign says Andrew Sneed was born and raised in Huntsville, graduated from Lee High, and later left restaurant work to start over as a plumber's helper. He founded Whole Home Solutions in 2019 and says the company now has several trucks and employees. He says he is running because the district needs a representative who is not a career politician. On health care, he says he wants to expand Medicaid, negotiate drug prices, regulate for-profit insurers, and keep rural hospitals open. On affordability, he says he wants to address housing, lower utility bills, and restore federal investment in energy efficiency. He also calls for congressional term limits, overturning Citizens United, a lobbying waiting period, and a ban on stock trading by members of Congress.

U.S. representative for Indianapolis and a former law enforcement officer. Born and raised in Indianapolis, he says he has focused on the economy, national security, and the middle class, and he serves on Intelligence, Transportation and Infrastructure, and a select committee on the Chinese Communist Party. He says he hosts an annual job fair and a youth opportunities fair. He says he would invest in early childhood and K-12 schools, raise teacher pay, and expand Pell Grants and workforce training as alternatives to a four-year degree. He says tariffs are raising household costs, and he wants tax cuts for working families, small businesses, and entrepreneurs rather than policy aimed at the ultra-wealthy. He says he opposes cuts to SNAP, introduced a Food Deserts Act to finance grocery stores in underserved areas, and supports military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine.

U.S. representative from Kentucky running for the Senate. Andy Barr's campaign calls him an eighth-generation Kentuckian and says he was the first member of the state's House delegation to endorse Donald Trump and chaired Trump's 2024 Kentucky primary campaign. He says he would deport people he calls criminal illegal immigrants, restart border-wall construction, hire more border agents, restore Remain in Mexico, and end catch-and-release. He says he voted for tax cuts that end taxes on Social Security for seniors, on overtime, and on tips, and he wants to expand Kentucky coal and block climate rules he says were imposed through financial regulators. He says he will defend girls' sports and private spaces, veterans' disability and health benefits, the Second Amendment, police funding, sanctions on fentanyl tied to China, and Kentucky farmers, including a federal framework for hemp products.

U.S. representative Andy Biggs is an Arizona native who has represented the state's 5th Congressional District since 2016. He is running for governor with Sine Kerr for lieutenant governor. He says he will eliminate the state income tax, work with local governments to ease property taxes, and cut permitting barriers for new homes. He says he will end state incentives for data centers and set standards to protect Arizona's water and energy. He says he will reconvene a Border Strike Force aimed at human trafficking and drug trafficking and equip police to fight drug trafficking.

Green Party candidate for governor of Maryland. Andy Ellis says he has lived in Baltimore since 2005, coached debate, and spent nearly 15 years in corporate technology. He says he has spent more than a decade organizing the Green Party in Baltimore and across Maryland. He says the state should stop data-center projects that he argues threaten communities, water, and public health. He says unaffiliated and third-party voters are shut out of meaningful elections and that he has a plan aimed at two-party political corruption. He says the state should spread wealth, power, and opportunity so more residents have a say in incentives, public funds, and budgets.

Physician and U.S. representative who chairs the House Freedom Caucus. The son of immigrants who fled communist Eastern Europe after World War II, he says he has been a Johns Hopkins physician, a Naval Reserve veteran, a state senator, and, since 2025, an eighth-term congressman. He chairs the Agriculture appropriations subcommittee. He says he is fighting to restore fiscal responsibility in Washington and protect taxpayer dollars. The campaign describes him as a common-sense conservative with the courage to change Washington. He says he is unafraid to speak for the priorities of Maryland's 1st District.

Community advocate running for Congress in Los Angeles. Angela Gonzales-Torres's campaign says she is a democratic socialist and a lifelong Angeleno from Highland Park, the daughter of a deportee who was raised by a single mother. It says she helps people leaving prison enter college and works on affordable housing that brings younger and older residents together. She says she would abolish ICE, make Los Angeles more affordable, and increase access to critical services. She says housing, health care, and education should be affordable, and she wants higher taxes on the wealthy to pay for them. She says she would abolish super PACs so elections answer to voters rather than donors.

Entrepreneur running for Congress. Angela Rodriguez Prilliman's campaign says she is a Fort Worth mother and entrepreneur who grew up in Stephenville, graduated from Texas A&M, and spent more than a decade in technology. It says she is the Democratic candidate in the 12th District. She says she would seek universal health care and universal child care, paid for by taxes on billionaires. She also lists voting rights, full funding for public schools, and getting billionaire money out of politics. She says Congress should protect AI whistleblowers, set liability and testing rules, and restrict AI companions for children.

Florida state representative and union organizer She says she is a state representative, union organizer, and mother who was born and raised in Jacksonville. She says she started as an organizer in Duval County and ran for office because she wanted more working people in government. She says she is running to lower costs, raise wages, and put working families ahead of billionaires. She says she supports Medicare for All and a national rent freeze with a moratorium on evictions. She says she supports free child care and pre-K, and a Working Families Guarantee for workers.

Neighborhood-council leader running for Congress. Angélica Dueñas's campaign says she was born in Sun Valley to parents who immigrated from Mexico, raised five children, and was the first in her family to finish college. It says she earned degrees from Cal State Los Angeles and Woodbury and served as president of the Sun Valley Area Neighborhood Council. She says she takes no corporate PAC, AIPAC, oil, or drug-company money, and she supports Medicare for All and housing as a right. She says she would abolish ICE, create a path to legal status, and pass the DREAM Act. She says she would raise the minimum wage, protect the right to unionize, and cancel student debt by making public college and trade school tuition-free.

U.S. representative for Missouri's 2nd District. She grew up working at her parents' carpet store in Manchester, studied business at the University of Missouri, and later held management jobs at Hallmark and Ralston Purina before coming to Congress. She says she has worked to cut taxes and regulation so local businesses can hire, and she voted for a tax bill that removes taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security. She highlights the Fight Online Sex Trafficking Act and funding for rape-kit testing through the Debbie Smith Act. She says she will keep defending a right to life, and she introduced a bill to require medical care for infants born alive after an abortion.

Faith leader and small-business owner running for Congress in Tennessee's 3rd District. Her campaign says she is a progressive faith leader who owns Biased Apparel and is chief executive of Work of Place, a firm that helps congregations use their buildings for neighbors' economic stability. She and her husband Mike live in Chattanooga's Park Central neighborhood. She says workers deserve wages that cover the bills and the freedom to organize, and that rural counties need funded hospitals, schools, and infrastructure. She says she takes no corporate PAC money and wants fair elections and fair maps. She says she would protect reproductive freedom and LGBTQ+ people, treat health care as a human right, and fund Oak Ridge's science without sacrificing the land.

U.S. representative running for another term. Anna Paulina Luna's campaign says she is a mother, Air Force veteran, and one of the younger members of Congress who did not grow up with wealth or a political family. It says her father struggled with substance abuse and her mother raised her on her own. She says big government is often the problem, not the solution, and that her politics come from growing up in hard circumstances and serving in the military. She says she wants reforms aimed at problems people actually face rather than an elitist approach to Congress.
Comptroller on the Kane County list and the Will County list. The lists do not state a party. A vote counts only where this declaration was filed.

Former Wayland selectwoman and business executive running for secretary of state. Anne Brensley's site says she is a former Wayland selectwoman, chief executive of DevCo North America, and was born in Honduras. She says she wants to encourage business growth. She says she will engage directly with disenfranchised voters. She says she will protect the integrity of the ballot and campaign on transparency and local control.

Pediatrician running for U.S. Senate Annie Andrews's campaign says she is a pediatrician and mother who has cared for South Carolina children for nearly twenty years, from newborns to teenagers. She says she is not a career politician. She says families are struggling with grocery prices, child care, and the cost of health care, and her platform treats health care as a right. Her listed plans include tackling debt and congressional perks, cutting taxes, lowering premiums, protecting rural hospitals, and reversing Medicaid cuts. The platform also lists strong schools and affordable child care, reproductive freedom, political corruption, and an end to gun violence.

Maryland attorney general, running for reelection. Anthony Brown's campaign says he is the state's attorney general, an Army veteran, and a lawyer raised by immigrant parents. It says that before this office he served in the legislature, as lieutenant governor, and in Congress. He says he created a civil-rights division and widened the Independent Investigations Division so it can prosecute police-involved deaths. He says he has defended gun-safety laws in court and pursued wage theft and corporate conduct that harms workers and consumers. He says he has sued when federal policy threatened environmental rules, voting rights, and protections for women and immigrants.
District 21 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Printing-company executive running for Congress in New York's 21st District. His campaign says he is the chief executive of Sticker Mule, an online printing company with plants in New York, South Carolina, and Italy. It says he is paying for the race himself so donors, lobbyists, and special interests will not have a claim on him. He says he would cut waste, bring reliable internet and cell service to the North Country, and oppose regulations he argues are driving up food and utility prices. He says he would work to secure the northern border, treat farmers more fairly, and restore First and Second Amendment rights he says have been restricted in New York.

Libertarian candidate for lieutenant governor. He says he is a high school English and debate teacher in Cibolo and a military veteran. He says he is running so Texans have a choice built on liberty, a balanced budget, and straight talk. He says real tax relief requires cutting spending, and that property-tax plans without spending cuts only move the bill somewhere else. He says he opposes taxpayer-funded welfare and supports immigrants who come to Texas to work. He says Texas should legalize marijuana and end what he calls the lieutenant governor's war on drugs.
District 1 · U.S. House · New Hampshire · Republican

Republican candidate for New Hampshire's 1st District. His campaign says his great-grandparents came through Ellis Island and that he came to the University of New Hampshire in 1983. He says he started a business with a small amount of cash and credit and now oversees more than 20 car dealerships and 11 collision centers employing about a thousand people. His plan leads with lower costs, higher wages, and a balanced-budget amendment. He says he will protect the 2017 tax cuts and the elimination of taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security, and fully support Social Security and Medicare. He calls for securing the southern and northern borders, a common-sense immigration reform, and defense of every law-abiding citizen's right to own a firearm.

Former Macomb County clerk, running for Michigan secretary of state. Anthony Forlini's campaign says he is a lifelong Michigan resident, a husband, father, and grandfather, and the son of an Italian immigrant. It says he has served as a township supervisor, a state representative, and Macomb County clerk. He says he would protect election integrity by removing ineligible and deceased voters from the rolls and by requiring watermarked ballots statewide. He says he would stop sending voter information to outside groups and audit county clerks so election practices match across the state. He says he would cut secretary of state wait times and make routine services easier to finish online or in person.

Candidate for governor of Michigan. Anthony Hudson's campaign says he was born and raised in Texas and moved to Michigan in 2012 to be in his children's lives. He describes himself as a blue-collar candidate running against what he calls corruption in Lansing. He says he would eliminate property taxes and the state income tax. He says he would stop data-center and solar-panel development and protect farmland. He says he wants lower taxes, smaller government, and decisions returned to local communities.

U.S. representative for Maryland's 6th District, seeking another term. Her campaign says she was raised in Buhl, Idaho, the daughter of a potato farmer, and is the mother of four. It says she led Common Sense Media's Washington office and served as a deputy assistant secretary for communications at the Department of Commerce. She says she will work on rising costs, health care, and equal access to a good education, and that she wants more job training, small-business support, and better-paying work in the district. She points to her work expanding broadband and says technology should drive development across the 6th District. She says she will put progress ahead of partisanship and defend democratic institutions.

Democrat running for Congress in Nebraska's 3rd District.
