U.S. representative running for another term. Gus Bilirakis's campaign says he is a Tampa Bay husband, father, and attorney whose father, Mike Bilirakis, represented the same community in Congress. It says he is a senior member of the Energy and Commerce Committee. He says he is taking on property-insurance costs, affordable housing, and the cost of living in Pasco and Hillsborough counties. He says he backed a larger senior tax exemption, no tax on tips or overtime, and a deduction for homeowners-insurance premiums.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 14th District. Guy Reschenthaler's campaign describes him as a son of western Pennsylvania who served in uniform and as a prosecutor and judge. He says he is running to keep the district's voice in Congress. His issues page says national security is personal because he prosecuted terrorists in Iraq, and that he supports a strong defense. He says cutting regulation in Harrisburg and Washington is how the region creates jobs, and he lists immigration, security, jobs, and taxes among his priorities.

U.S. representative and the first African American woman Wisconsin elected to the House. She took the oath on January 4, 2005, later co-chaired the 2020 Democratic National Convention in Milwaukee, and has chaired the Congressional Women's Caucus. She says serving the 4th District is the privilege of a lifetime. The campaign calls her a champion for working Wisconsinites and a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. It says she has been a champion for protecting Social Security and Medicare and an advocate for low-income communities. It says she is a voice against what it calls an assault on democracy.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.
District 8 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

House Democratic leader representing New York's 8th District. His campaign says he has represented the Brooklyn-based district since 2013 and was elected House Democratic leader in 2023, the first person of color to lead a major party in Congress. It says the district includes neighborhoods such as East New York, Brownsville, Bedford-Stuyvesant, Canarsie, and Coney Island. He says he is working to lower child care, health care, education, and prescription costs, including a $35 monthly insulin cap for people on Medicare. He supports universal background checks and a ban on assault weapons, and he highlights a law that made gun trafficking a federal crime. He says he wants more affordable and public housing, better-paying jobs through infrastructure and manufacturing investment, and protection of abortion access.

Dean of the U.S. House, representing southern and eastern Kentucky since 1981. Born in rural Kentucky, he says he has been elected to 23 consecutive terms and became the longest-serving House member in 2022. He points to Operation UNITE, the Center for Rural Development, and SOAR as regional projects he helped build. He says that as Appropriations chair from 2011 to 2016 he cut discretionary spending by $126 billion and pushed oversight of federal agencies. He says he led the first Homeland Security appropriations subcommittee and pressed for immigration enforcement and border security. After winning the 2026 primary he said he would keep fighting for conservative values, jobs at home, and energy independence.

Sixth-generation farmer Hallie Shoffner says she is a sixth-generation Arkansas farmer and that she has lived through a farm shutdown. She describes the farming community of Shoffner, named for her family, as a place that is now empty buildings and abandoned fields. She says she will cut taxes for working families and lower the cost of groceries, child care, housing, and health care. She says she will protect and strengthen Social Security and Medicare, lift the payroll-tax cap on the very wealthy, and reverse cuts to those programs. She says a farm bill should help farmers diversify, sell into regional markets, and supply food to public schools.

U.S. representative for Georgia's 4th District. His campaign says he is in his tenth term representing parts of DeKalb and Gwinnett counties, and it describes him as a legislator focused on delivering results for the district. He says he supports DACA, temporary protected status, refugees, and immigrants who come to build a better life for their children. He says he has delivered more than $350 million in federal investment for district job creation since January 2009, including $98 million he says saved more than 1,000 teaching jobs in DeKalb, Rockdale, Newton, and Gwinnett counties. He says he will oppose efforts to take away affordable health insurance and will stand with consumers seeking coverage.

Candidate for governor of Maine. Hannah Pingree says she was raised on the island of North Haven, became Speaker of the Maine House, and later directed the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future. She says she still lives on North Haven with her husband and two children. She says her record includes expanding access to health care and affordable housing and helping lead the state's climate work. She says that in the Legislature she worked on rural broadband, clean energy, lower health costs, reproductive rights, and Maine's working waterfronts. She says that work included the Kid-Safe Products Act, aimed at keeping toxic chemicals out of products children use.

Member of Congress and lawyer whose campaign says she has fought federal regulators in court. Her campaign says she has spent her career challenging rules that affect ranchers, farmers, and energy producers, and that Congress should take back power it has given to federal agencies. She says she will defend speech, gun rights, and private property, and that she wants voter identification and an end to mailing ballots to people who did not request them. She says she will fight tax increases, cut federal spending, and defend oil, gas, and coal production. She says federal land agencies have mismanaged forests and that she wants multiple-use rules that answer to the people who live with those decisions.
Secretary of State · South Dakota · Republican

State representative and small-business owner Heather Baxter's campaign says she has been the state representative for District 34 since November 2024 and owns a small business in Rapid City and Custer. She says she is a lifelong South Dakotan running for secretary of state. She says she would push secure and transparent elections and restore trust in how votes are run. She says she would give small businesses easier access to office resources and cut red tape through what she calls SD DOGE. She says she would improve customer service in the secretary of state's office.

Retired Ford employee running for Congress in Michigan's 6th District. Her campaign says she is a Christian mother of two, married 30 years, and the first in her family to attend college, earning a bachelor's and a master's from Central Michigan University. She says she recently retired from Ford after more than 32 years in product development, planning, and analytics. She says she would cut wasteful spending, balance the budget, and limit spending bills that bundle unrelated items. She wants schools focused on academics, elections limited to citizens, and energy independence through the free market. She says she would close the border, protect the right to self-defense, and restrict foreign ownership of land.

Candidate for Congress in Tennessee's 8th District. Her campaign says the district needs fresh ideas and leaders who show up for people, and she is asking voters to make a plan for Election Day. She says data centers should not get a blank check. She says communities deserve a say in whether and where data centers are built, and in how much water and power they use.

Former CVS retail president running for governor Helena Foulkes's campaign says she is a lifelong Rhode Islander who spent 25 years at CVS and became president of its retail division. It says that as retail president she worked to lower prescription prices and took tobacco off the shelves. She says she would create good-paying jobs and make Rhode Island more affordable, and she criticizes the state's handling of housing and the Washington Bridge. She says she would push back against federal funding cuts aimed at states like Rhode Island. Her plans page lists health care, jobs, child care and transportation, career and technical education, and a housing program called Rhode Home.

U.S. representative and former Texas secretary of state. His official biography says he was born in Laredo, the eldest of eight children of migrant farmworkers, and was the first in his family to attend college. He has worked as a lawyer, customs broker, and educator, and served as a state representative and Texas secretary of state. He says education is the key that opens the door to opportunity for every child. He says his Appropriations work, including as ranking member of the Homeland Security Subcommittee, is meant to strengthen national security while delivering results for South Texas. He says a bipartisan reputation keeps him at the table fighting for Texas families no matter which party is in power.
District 3 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Democratic

Physician and U.S. representative for New Jersey's 3rd District. His campaign says he is a lifelong Burlington County resident, the son of a teacher and a nurse, who earned degrees from Princeton, Jefferson Medical College, and Rutgers Law School. He says he served 25 years in the Assembly, including as health committee chair, before his first term in Congress. He says government does not belong in the exam room and that he is fighting to keep health care, including abortion, affordable. He says he wants safe communities, strong public schools, good jobs, and a healthy environment. He says he has worked to ease taxes on middle-class families, protect small businesses, and open manufacturing pathways for students.

County supervisor and former labor secretary running for Congress. Hilda Solis's campaign says she has stood up for working people as a county supervisor and is now running for the House. It says she served as secretary of labor in President Obama's Cabinet and helped implement the Affordable Care Act. She says she is running to defend workers, immigrants, educators, affordable housing, reproductive rights, veterans, unions, Medicaid, and democracy. She says she has prioritized clean air, water, and open space, and she cites environmental-justice laws recognized with a Profile in Courage award. She says she wants to create and preserve affordable housing and find better ways to help people who are homeless.
District 6 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Republican

Civil servant running for Congress in New Jersey's 6th District. Her campaign says she is a Monmouth County mother of three and the spouse of an Army veteran, with a criminal-justice degree and years of civil service in police, military, veterans, agriculture, and immigration agencies. She says she attended school in New Jersey and is running because the district needs new leadership. She says she will fight for parental rights and transparency in education, lower taxes, and medical freedom. She says she wants fair immigration reform, respect for veterans and seniors, and clean water and air. She also lists equal rights and expanded liberty under the Constitution.

U.S. representative for Michigan's 3rd District. Her campaign says she is a former Justice Department attorney, a Christian, and a mother of two, and that in 2022 she became the first Democratic woman to represent West Michigan in the House. She says she is running for a third term focused on costs, health care, and government corruption. She says she is working to lower health-care and drug costs, defend the Affordable Care Act, and stop insurers from dropping people who get sick. She says decisions about pregnancy belong with women, and that she will protect the right to choose. She wants well-paying jobs, semiconductor manufacturing in Michigan, and protection of drinking water from PFAS.

South Bay native and Marine Corps veteran running for Congress. Houston Brignano's campaign says he was born and raised in the South Bay, joined the Marine Corps out of high school, and deployed twice to Iraq. It says he and his wife are raising three daughters there and that they homeschool. He says student debt and housing costs, including a first-time homebuyer age he puts at 40, are shutting people out of a stable life. He says he would train young people to use artificial intelligence and protect jobs from automation with reskilling programs.

Georgia state representative running for Congress. He says he was born and raised in Athens, where he still lives, and has served in the State House since 2019 for Barrow, Clarke, Jackson, and Oconee counties. He says his work has been helping small businesses grow, and that he now works with Carter Engineering in Oconee County. He says immigration enforcement should keep cooperating with ICE, deportations should continue, and the border should stay secured. He says he led opposition to defunding the police in Georgia, backed hundreds of millions of dollars for law enforcement, and took on district attorneys he says endangered public safety. He wants spending cuts and tax cuts to match what he calls Georgia's balanced budgets, more American manufacturing, a military rebuilt around strength, and a block on Chinese purchases of U.S. farmland.

U.S. representative and the first African refugee elected to Congress. She says her public service started at 14 interpreting for her grandfather at DFL caucuses, and that in 2016 she became the first Somali-American Muslim legislator in the country. In 2018 she became the first woman of color to represent Minnesota in Congress. She says she has fought to codify Roe v. Wade, pass climate legislation, address opioids, and ban assault weapons. She says she negotiated a public-safety bill with local investment and accountability, and funding that fed more than 30 million children during the pandemic. She says community projects she brought home include veteran housing in Robbinsdale and help for entrepreneurs in north Minneapolis.

Incumbent since 2019, with Christian Mitchell, a former state representative and deputy governor Businessman seeking a third term, which no Illinois Democrat has won. Mitchell would replace Stratton, who is running for Senate. This guide has no separate photo of Mitchell. Pritzker campaigns on wages, abortion access, schools, and budgets he says are balanced, along with credit-rating upgrades. Points to the $15 minimum wage, the ended state grocery tax, a doubled child tax credit, a $35 insulin cap, and medical-debt relief. Wants more housing. Abortion-access laws that made Illinois a destination for care. He says health care is a right and opposes federal Medicaid cuts. Signed limits on civil immigration arrests near courthouses, hospitals, colleges, and day cares. Says people convicted of violent crimes should be deported, and that he is open to changes in SAFE-T pretrial rules.

Indiana state senator running for Congress in the 5th District. He says he entered the state Senate in 2018, flipped a long-held Republican district, and is the first openly LGBTQ+ legislator in Indiana history. He says he is not independently wealthy and knows the pressure of rising health-care and grocery costs. He says he would cap health-care and prescription costs and push corporations to account for prices on groceries, housing, and energy. He says Washington needs a Democratic check so federal agencies are not above the law. He says he grew up in a union family, with a father who drove trucks and a mother who was a school secretary, and that he is running because that middle-class promise is no longer guaranteed.

Air Force officer and lawyer running for Congress. Jace Yarbrough's campaign says he is a seventh-generation Texan, an Air Force major, and a constitutional lawyer with degrees from UT Austin and Stanford. It says he and his wife founded a classical Christian school and are raising five children. He says he would back immigration enforcement and oppose amnesty, and keep legal immigration from being used to push down wages. He says he would seek national concealed-carry reciprocity and repeal of the National Firearms Act.

U.S. representative and retired Marine lieutenant general. His campaign says he rose to lieutenant general in the Marine Corps, ran a small business, and spent 22 years as a commercial airline pilot. He and his wife Cindy live in Watersmeet, and the campaign says family roots in the Upper Peninsula go back to iron miners in the late 1800s. He says he has worked to expand rural broadband, including a bill that would account for short construction seasons in northern Michigan. He says his veterans work includes suicide-prevention grants, more home and community care, and a burial-benefit fix he calls Gerald's Law. He says he backs Michigan farms, including cherry growers, opposes taxpayer funding of abortion, and wants a military strong enough to deter adversaries.
District 12 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Republican

Financial professional running for Congress in North Carolina's 12th District. His campaign says he is a Christian and a financial professional who decided to run because of housing costs, personal debt, and what he calls an erosion of civility. He says America should work for everyone. He pledges not to accept PAC money and not to trade individual stocks. He says he would hold more than 10 town halls a year.

U.S. senator Jack Reed's campaign says he grew up in Cranston, graduated from West Point, served as an Army Ranger, and commanded paratroopers in the 82nd Airborne. It says he serves on the Appropriations and Armed Services committees. He says he voted against the Iraq War, opposes the Iran war, and is using his Senate vote to stop that war and other military operations he calls unnecessary. He says he wants housing, education, health care, and environmental spending paid for by higher taxes on billionaires and changes to the tax system. He says he has worked to bring federal money to Rhode Island for housing, coastal research, Coast Guard ships, Quonset jobs, the airport, roads, and transit.
District 18 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Hudson Valley resident running for Congress in New York's 18th District. Her campaign says she was born in the Hudson Valley and is running because the region is becoming too expensive for the families who built it. It says she is not a career politician and does not owe favors to party bosses or special interests. She says she would work on taxes, energy, everyday bills, and health care so more income stays with families and small businesses. She says she would focus on good-paying jobs, skilled trades, and education connected to careers in the region. She also calls for congressional ethics, government transparency, and protection of local rights and public safety.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

State assemblymember running for Congress. Jacqui Irwin's campaign says she is a mother, an engineer, and a community leader with two decades in local public life. It says she is running for the new 26th District to focus on public safety, affordability, and Ventura and Los Angeles counties. She says she would stand up for the district against what she calls an assault on democracy and California values. Her campaign highlights laws she wrote on housing and services for homeless veterans, a state climate law, and gun-safety measures. It says she has worked to create jobs, balance budgets, and keep communities safe.

U.S. representative for Connecticut's 5th District The campaign says Jahana Hayes, a teacher named National Teacher of the Year in 2016, was elected in 2018 as Connecticut's first African American congresswoman. She sits on Education and Labor and on Agriculture, where she is ranking member of the nutrition subcommittee. She supports Medicare for All and says she has worked to curb surprise bills and cap prescription drug costs. She wants housing help for first-time buyers and an economy that lowers grocery, gas, and energy costs rather than serving only the very wealthy. She supports red-flag laws, expanded background checks, and other steps to reduce gun violence.

Marine and U.S. representative on the Energy and Commerce Committee. He says he is a dad, a Marine, and a lifelong student of American history who represents 35 cities and towns from Fall River to Brookline. He says leaders fight from the front, own hard decisions, and eat last. He says he works in Washington to defend democracy and lower prices against corruption that makes the American dream too expensive. He describes a New American Dream as an excellent education by 18, a home by 30, and a dignified retirement by 65. He says housing, health care, and utility costs should be treated by cutting rules that block starter homes, using technology to lower hospital prices, and fixing Social Security so the wealthiest pay more in.

U.S. representative running for another term. Jake Ellzey's campaign says he is a Naval Academy graduate who flew fighters, served on the ground with a SEAL team, and finished as air boss on the USS Ronald Reagan. He says Congress should finish a border wall, back Border Patrol, and stop projects he says seize private land, including a proposed high-speed rail. Math teacher running for Congress. Jake Johnson's site says he grew up in Stewartville, is a math teacher and father of four, and that he and his wife Molly, a paraprofessional, are raising their boys in southern Minnesota. He says he will vote to end tariffs and the Iran war that he says are raising grocery, gas, and fertilizer prices, cut taxes for working families, and raise taxes on big corporations and the very wealthy. He says he supports a balanced-budget amendment, term limits, a ban on members of Congress trading stocks or becoming lobbyists, and recovering money lost to fraud in Minnesota. Lawyer and former deputy prosecutor running for Congress. She says gas, groceries, housing, utilities, and health care should be affordable, and that tax dollars should go to Indiana families rather than Wall Street or endless foreign conflicts. Wyoming legislator running for the U.S. Senate. He says he will keep public lands public and open for hunting, fishing, grazing, and recreation, rather than selling them.

U.S. representative and chair of the House Oversight Committee. California assemblymember running for Congress. He says he would defend property rights and parental rights and shield farms and businesses from excessive regulation.

Economist running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 12th District. He says he is running for safer communities, stronger growth, and practical leadership. He says he wants less regulation, a return of good-paying union jobs, support for law enforcement, and accountability for repeat violent offenders. He also supports school choice, an all-of-the-above energy strategy, standing with allies including Israel, and reining in federal spending.

Building-trades worker running for Congress in Michigan's 12th District. His campaign says he grew up on the east side of Detroit, worked at Eastern Market, and later worked in the building trades. He says he is pro-life from conception to natural death and that the Second Amendment should not be infringed. He says he is a conservative Christian and that he will be a voice for those positions in the House.

U.S. representative and chair of the House Rules Committee. Born and raised in Worcester, he is the son of small-business owners and has represented the 2nd District since 1996. Attorney and Democratic nominee for Florida's 11th District His campaign says that over more than 30 years he has served as a presidential appointee in the Clinton administration, a congressional staff member, an attorney, and a government-affairs executive. Mental health business owner running for Congress The campaign says James Russell, who goes by Rus, has lived in central Arkansas for more than 25 years with his wife, Wendy, and they have run an outpatient mental health business in Little Rock since 2014. Candidate for Maryland attorney general. Jim Rutledge's campaign says he earned a law degree with honors from the University of Maryland and has practiced law in Maryland for decades. Candidate for the U.S. Senate. His campaign says he is an eighth-generation Texan, a former middle school teacher, and a Presbyterian seminarian who has served as a state representative. Attorney General of Florida He says he previously served as Governor Ron DeSantis's chief of staff and, before that, as counsel to Donald Trump's 2016 campaign and as a senior advisor to Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross. U.S. representative for Virginia's 11th District. He says he grew up in Prince William County, graduated from NYU, and lives in Fairfax with his wife, Yvette, and their son, Mateo. He also says his work includes protecting federal workers, health care, Social Security and Medicare, and lowering costs for northern Virginia.

Republican nominee for Colorado secretary of state. Researcher running for Congress. U.S. representative for Maryland's 8th District, sworn in for a fifth term in 2025. D.C. Councilmember for Ward 4 She says she is a third-generation Washingtonian raised in Ward 4, a graduate of D.C. public schools and Howard University School of Law, and a former assistant attorney general who was elected to the Council in 2020. U.S. representative for Oregon's 5th District, seeking another term. Journalist running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 10th District. Janelle Stelson says she spent more than 30 years telling stories in central Pennsylvania. Independent American candidate for lieutenant governor. Janine Hansen says she is a native Nevadan who has advocated for families and taxpayers at the Legislature throughout her adult life. U.S. representative running for another term. He says he has pushed federal money for local infrastructure, tribal clean energy and broadband, salmon habitat, and toxic-site cleanup. U.S. representative for Florida's 25th District His campaign says he was born and raised in Broward County, graduated from Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, and joined the Parkland City Commission while in law school at Nova Southeastern. He and his wife, Leah, live in Broward with their two sons. He says he wrote legislation to cut property-insurance premiums and is fighting prescription prices, housing costs, and price gouging. He says he would protect Social Security and Medicare and reverse Medicaid cuts. He says that after the 2018 shooting at his high school he helped pass Florida's school-safety law, and that he supports a ban on members of Congress trading stocks.

His listed plans include cutting energy costs, teaching artificial intelligence in every high school by 2028, capping out-of-pocket health costs, and building 20,000 housing units in four years.

Microbiologist and Georgia state representative running for Congress. Her agenda lists lowering the cost of living, protecting education at every stage, and building an economy that works for people. She also lists protecting rights and the most vulnerable, building safer communities, protecting democracy, and supporting veterans. Small-business owner running for U.S. House in Colorado's 6th District. Combat veteran running for Congress. Jason Crow's campaign says he grew up in a working-class family, the grandson of a bricklayer and the son of small-business owners. Constitutional advocate running for Michigan attorney general. He says he founded WTPN.news to publish the same record on candidates, donors, and officials, including himself. He says he would back law enforcement and end what he calls catch-and-release treatment of repeat offenders. He says he is running to put local values and practical problem-solving ahead of party politics.

Plano native and former mortgage and insurance worker running for Congress. His campaign says he was born and raised in Plano, started working as a kid, and often worked two jobs and 80-hour weeks. U.S. representative for Missouri's 8th District. Former NFL kicker running for Congress in Arizona's 1st District. His campaign says he played 14 seasons in the NFL, including for the Arizona Cardinals, and later worked as a CBS analyst. Software entrepreneur and U.S. representative running for another term. He says he is fighting to balance the federal budget and stop spending he argues is driving up prices. He says he has worked to lower taxes, repeal gas taxes, help small businesses, and expand the child tax credit. He says he wrote a bill to hold fentanyl dealers accountable, voted to fund the military and a border-security bill, and wants the border wall finished.

Wisconsin native and business graduate running for secretary of state. U.S. representative for Colorado's 5th District. Jeff Crank says he was born and raised in southern Colorado and has spent more than 30 years working to strengthen El Paso County. Small-business owner running for Congress. Jeff Frese's campaign says he is a husband, father, and coach in Moraga who built a national snack brand from his kitchen and has run consumer companies. Grand Junction attorney running for U.S. House in Colorado's 3rd District. Lawyer and former state representative Jeff McLaughlin was a schoolteacher, then practiced law in Guntersville for more than 30 years, and represented Marshall County in the Alabama House for ten of those years. U.S. senator from Oregon, seeking another term. His campaign says he was born in Myrtle Creek and has not lost touch with working-class roots. Democratic candidate for Mississippi's 4th District. U.S. representative, former Navy pilot, and nurse practitioner. Teacher running for Congress in Ohio's 2nd District. Jen Mazzuckelli says she was raised by a teacher and a federal employee, earned an English degree and a master's in teaching, and worked as a high school English teacher. She says she is in long-term recovery, has multiple sclerosis, and has lived through domestic violence. She says the representative should work for the people rather than campaign donors, and that neighbors who disagree are not enemies. She says public servants should keep promises and that the way to earn reelection is to do the job well.

Colorado secretary of state running for attorney general. Jena Griswold says she grew up in a working-class family in Estes Park, was the first in her family to attend a four-year college, and earned a law degree. She says she has been secretary of state since 2018 and is running for attorney general to stand up to Donald Trump and protect Coloradans' rights. She says she will defend the rights and freedoms of Coloradans and will not be intimidated. She says that as secretary of state she backed laws against threats to election workers, guns near voting centers, and tampering with voting equipment. She says she expanded ballot drop boxes, in-person voting, campus and tribal voting access, and automatic voter registration.

Educator and former Oklahoma Teacher of the Year running for Congress. Her campaign says she taught for more than 16 years, was Oklahoma Teacher of the Year in 2020, and later worked in nonprofit and corporate leadership, including at the Oklahoma Faith Network. She says she and her husband Karl have two children, and that in 2022 she received more votes than any other Democrat in the race for state superintendent. She says Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid should be protected and strengthened, and that Medicare should negotiate lower drug prices. She says a secure border and a fair immigration system both matter, with more agents and sensors against drug trafficking, faster asylum decisions, and more work visas. She says she would expose backroom deals and opposes adding trillions to the deficit to pay for tax breaks for the wealthiest.
District 11 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Republican

State representative and mortgage lender running for Congress in North Carolina's 11th District. Her campaign says she is an eighth-generation western North Carolinian who grew up on her family's apple farm in Henderson County and has worked in banking since 1998. She says she is a mortgage loan officer who represents Henderson County in the state House and lives in Hendersonville. She says working families should be able to own a home and keep more of what they earn. She says she supports local credit unions and helped change state law so more rural towns can be served by them. She says she supports ending the state income tax on tips, overtime, and bonuses.

Former state representative running for secretary of state. Jennifer Day's site says she has 16 years of business experience in technology, real estate, and finance, founded an interior-design company, worked eight years as an election worker, and represented Kansas House District 48. She says voting systems should stay accurate and free of disinformation, and that she will coordinate with county election officials. She says she will look at states with higher turnout and consider similar ways to bring eligible Kansans into voting. She says she will keep modernizing business registration so it is easier to start and run a company.

Former school board member and Democratic nominee for Florida's 8th District Her campaign says she is the daughter of a corrections officer and a mother living with a disability, grew up in a working-class family, and built a career in education. She served on the Brevard County School Board and, in 2020, defeated a co-founder of Moms for Liberty. She lives in Satellite Beach with her husband, a middle-school teacher, and their daughter. She says she would stabilize Florida property insurance with federal reinsurance and oppose tariffs that raise the price of everyday goods. She says she would expand Medicaid, restore Affordable Care Act subsidies, and protect coverage for pre-existing conditions. She says she would protect the Department of Education, fully fund special-education law, and invest in teachers and student mental health.

U.S. representative for Virginia's 4th District. Jennifer McClellan's office says she entered Congress in 2023 after a special election and was the first Black woman elected to Congress from Virginia. Born in Petersburg, she was valedictorian of Matoaca High School and earned degrees from the University of Richmond and the University of Virginia School of Law. She served in the Virginia House beginning in 2005 and the State Senate beginning in 2017, and she lives in Richmond with her husband David Mills and their two children. She says that on the Energy and Commerce Committee she works on access to health care, lower energy bills, and a clean and livable planet. She says that in the General Assembly she passed bills to protect and expand voting rights, combat climate change, preserve reproductive health care, and strengthen worker protections.
District 10 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Republican candidate for New York's 10th District. Her campaign says she is a lifelong Brooklynite who got on the ballot to give voters a choice after Brad Lander won the Democratic primary. She is the Republican and Conservative nominee for a district that includes parts of Brooklyn and Lower Manhattan. She says she will support the NYPD and first responders and reject policies she says have made streets less safe. She says New Yorkers are being priced out of their neighborhoods and wants practical answers to the cost of living. She says she will stand for working families, parents, and small-business owners.
District 1 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Republican

Attorney, small-business owner, and local Republican official running for Congress. Her campaign says she is a wife, mother, attorney, small-business owner, girls' sports coach, and lifelong Lowcountry resident who has held local elected office. She says that in office she has balanced budgets, stood with law enforcement, and defended the Constitution. She says she would put the Lowcountry first, stand with law enforcement, and secure the border against fentanyl and people she calls criminal illegal aliens. She says she would fight wasteful spending, balance the budget, and defend the Constitution, including free speech, religious liberty, and the Second Amendment. She says she would protect the unborn, keep men out of women's sports, lower family costs, and press for veterans' health care, benefits, jobs, and housing with less red tape.

Business owner running for Congress in California's 47th District. Her campaign says she co-built companies in energy and financial services, then bought and ran a technology services firm. She has an economics degree from the University of Virginia and an MBA from Columbia, and she is executive director of CAL DOGE, the office she says has gone through California spending line by line. She says she will cut waste and fraud so groceries, gas, insurance, and rent cost less. She says federal housing money should go first to cities that cut permit delays and fees, and that energy should be produced onshore rather than drilled off Orange County. She says she will fully fund border security, end catch-and-release, and require federal homelessness grants to show they get people off the street.

Independent candidate for the U.S. Senate. He says he is an independent running with a plan he calls American, and that he wants voters of every party involved. He says supporters may mail a one-dollar pledge and that unused campaign money will be returned on request. He lists his priorities as defending the Constitution, clarifying history, and restoring what he calls equality for people. He says he would draft an Equal Earnings Act and use assets at Fort Knox toward legislation and the national debt. He says he wants economic alternatives to war and protection of what he calls American human freedom.

State Senate president pro tem running for Congress in Michigan's 11th District. His campaign says he is a lifelong Oakland County resident, a Groves High School and Michigan State graduate, and that Southfield voters elected him to the city council in 2011. He says he later led the 2022 campaign that flipped the Michigan Senate and now serves as president pro tem. He says he would lower everyday costs, push back on tariffs he says raise prices, and defend Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid. He says he reduced barriers to voting as elections committee chair, strengthened the state civil-rights law, and acted to protect abortion access after Roe was overturned. He says he passed gun-safety laws, restored labor rights, and returned tax relief to seniors and working families.

State representative running for governor Jermaine Johnson's campaign says he is a state representative who has passed bills on the senior sales tax, a closed bridge, and broadband. The site also introduces Sam Skardon as his lieutenant-governor running mate. He says he would expand the number of families who owe no income tax rather than eliminate the tax, because he says ending it would mainly help the wealthiest, and he says he would work with cities to cut property taxes. He says he would let cities fix roads with transportation-department money, raise law-enforcement pay, and fund more rural hospitals and trade schools. He says he would audit public education, protect reproductive decisions for patients and doctors, and legalize medical marijuana while putting recreational use to a statewide vote.

Navy veteran and software engineer running for Congress in Ohio's 12th District. Jerrad Christian says he is a Navy veteran who served as a meteorologist, a software engineer, and someone who grew up with poverty in rural Ohio. He says that service turned him into an advocate for using less oil. He wants to overturn the Citizens United ruling, cap campaign spending, and stop foreign-linked money in elections. He also supports universal health care, a higher minimum wage, and more housing by changing exclusionary zoning and limiting large corporate buyers.

Candidate for governor of Tennessee. She describes herself as a lifelong Tennessean, a lawyer, an educator, and a mother of three who has lived in Memphis, Nashville, and Knoxville. She says her public work has included public defense, the Memphis City Council, and county government. She says she will expand paid family and medical leave, support collective bargaining, and invest in small businesses, especially in underserved areas. She says public schools should be fully funded, with respected teachers and without what she calls censorship and political interference. She says the state should expand Medicaid, especially in rural Tennessee, and she supports background checks, red-flag laws, and gun locks.

Businessman and former Mobile County commissioner running for Congress The campaign says Jerry Carl was born in Mobile, started his first company at 25, and has launched more than ten businesses over four decades, from real estate and health care to timber. He later served on the Mobile County Commission, where the campaign says he voted against tax increases and skipped a taxpayer-funded salary for his first two years. He says he will work with President Trump on an America First agenda. He says illegal immigration threatens national security and points to border-wall funding and more Border Patrol agents as work he wants continued. He says he is a lifelong hunter who will defend the Second Amendment.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Healthcare worker running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 2nd District. Jessica Arriaga is a mother from North Philadelphia who has worked in operating rooms for more than 20 years. She says she is running to put results for the city ahead of party politics. She says public safety, the cost of living, and career and technical education are the issues she hears about most. She argues health care should put patients first and that the city needs practical results rather than partisan fights.

Former Justice Department official running for Congress. Jessica Hart Steinmann's campaign says she is a Christian, a wife, and a mother of two who served in the Trump Justice Department as director of the Office for Victims of Crime. It says she later was executive general counsel at the America First Policy Institute and is the Trump-endorsed Republican for the 8th District. She says she would put Texas and American workers ahead of what she calls global elites, secure the border, and defend the Constitution. She says she has fought diversity programs in higher education, represented service members who challenged a COVID vaccine mandate, and sued to keep boys out of girls' sports. She says parents, not government, should direct how children are raised, and that she led federal work against human trafficking.

Army veteran running for U.S. House in Colorado's 5th District. Jessica Killin says she is a fourth-generation Coloradan, raised in Colorado Springs by two public-school educators, who served as an Army captain and military police officer. She says she later spent more than a decade at USAA on policy for military families, then worked on Capitol Hill and at the White House, and that this is her first campaign for office. She says she would lower costs for housing, groceries, health care, and energy, strengthen VA care, and cut federal spending that does not work. She says she would end tariffs that raise everyday prices, limit corporate landlords, and hold monopoly utilities accountable for high electric bills. She says she would ban members of Congress from trading stocks, support term limits, and let Medicare negotiate prices on more drugs.

U.S. representative for Hawaii's 2nd District The campaign says Jill Tokuda is a lifelong Kaneohe resident who represented Kaneohe and Kailua in the state Senate from 2006 to 2018, including as Ways and Means chair, and was first elected to Congress in 2022. She sits on Agriculture and Armed Services and co-chairs the Bipartisan Rural Health Caucus. She says zip code and income should not decide the quality of care, and she wants rural hospitals, mobile clinics, telehealth, and Medicare for All. She says she is fighting tariffs, wants the federal gas tax suspended, and wants childcare and the child tax credit expanded so families can stay in Hawaii. She says getting sick should not push people into debt.

U.S. representative for Indiana's 4th District. His office says he is a lifelong resident of west-central Indiana, a Purdue graduate in animal science, and a Vietnam veteran who received a Bronze Star and two Purple Hearts. He farmed and ran a home health agency, served as a Putnam County commissioner and for eight years in the Indiana House, and sits on the Agriculture, Foreign Affairs, and Science committees. He and his wife, Danise, have three children. He says his priorities are protecting family farms, cutting federal spending, and expanding rural health care through more competition and telehealth. He says he would secure the southern border and give immigration enforcement the resources to remove people here illegally who have committed crimes. He says he would protect Second Amendment rights and support veterans.
District 6 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Democratic

U.S. representative for South Carolina's 6th District since 1993. His official biography says he grew up in Sumter as the son of a minister and a beautician, graduated from South Carolina State, and taught school in Charleston before becoming the first Black advisor to a South Carolina governor and later Human Affairs commissioner. He is a former House majority whip and now ranking member of an Appropriations subcommittee. He says his 10-20-30 formula sends at least 10 percent of certain funds to communities where 20 percent or more of people have lived in poverty for 30 years. He points to his Rural Energy Savings Program, which lets rural electric cooperatives lend for home energy efficiency, and to a broadband bill funded in the 2021 infrastructure law. His biography says he has worked to make America's greatness accessible and affordable, including preserving historic buildings at historically Black colleges and creating heritage corridors and parks.

Farmer and U.S. representative running for another term. Jim Costa's campaign describes him as a farmer and member of Congress whose priority is the future of the San Joaquin Valley. It says his work has centered on water, health care, crime, and veterans. He says he helped win federal money for drinking water, aging water projects, storage, highways, and wildfire risk reduction. He says he has funded hospitals, community clinics, and a Valley medical school, and sought more officers to fight gangs and drugs. He says he has defended Dreamers, opposed family separations, and supports a path to citizenship.

County supervisor, pilot, and former mayor running for Congress. Jim Desmond's campaign says he is a father, a husband, a Navy veteran, a Delta Air Lines pilot for 33 years, a former mayor of San Marcos, and a San Diego County supervisor. He says he is running to bring common sense back to government and to focus on fixing problems. He says it is time for common sense to return to government and for leaders to fix problems. His site lists the cost of living, homelessness, the border, energy, and vocational and military education among his priorities.

Navy veteran and businessman running for Congress in Georgia's 4th District. His campaign says he grew up with very little, served in the Navy's nuclear submarine force, and then built a business. He describes himself as a husband, father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, and not a career politician. He says he supports the FairTax Act, H.R. 25, which would end the federal income, payroll, estate, and gift taxes, abolish the IRS, and replace them with a national sales tax plus a monthly rebate so households at or below the poverty level pay no net federal tax. He says families should be able to go to school, church, and the store without fear, and he would back law enforcement and first responders. He says he would cut regulations that make it harder for small businesses to hire and grow, and defend the Second Amendment, religious liberty, and free speech.

U.S. representative for Connecticut's 4th District The campaign says Jim Himes has represented Connecticut's 4th District since his election in 2008. Born in Peru to American parents, he later attended Harvard, studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, worked at Goldman Sachs, and then led a nonprofit office that financed affordable housing in the New York area. He says he is fighting for accessible, affordable health care and to protect Social Security. He says he is taking on the gun lobby to reduce gun violence and wants more economic opportunity for working families. As the lead Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, he says he works against foreign and domestic interference and for peaceful transfers of power.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 4th District and chair of the House Judiciary Committee. His campaign says he was a state and college wrestling champion, grew up in rural Champaign County, and was the first chair of the House Freedom Caucus. It says his focus in Congress is oversight of federal agencies. He says he is using the Judiciary Committee to investigate federal agencies, including the IRS, and to defend constitutional freedoms. He points to a Cut, Cap and Balance plan and says he has offered deep spending cuts and a balanced federal budget. The campaign says that as a state legislator he opposed higher taxes and spending and received awards from Ohio anti-abortion groups.

Insurance professional running for Congress in Georgia's 1st District. He calls himself a lifelong son of southeast Georgia, raised on faith, family, and service. He says his insurance career showed him how federal red tape holds back small towns, farms, and growing communities, and he describes himself as a Trump conservative. He says he will fight to lower taxes so families and small businesses keep more of what they earn, and he wants regular appropriations, balanced budgets, and agency accountability for spending. On health programs, he supports work requirements for able-bodied Medicaid adults, says Medicaid should not cover people in the country illegally, and says he will protect Medicare while rooting out waste and giving seniors more control of their care. He says he is running to defend President Trump, make the district more affordable, and back border enforcement.

Candidate for secretary of state. Jim Marchant says he is running for secretary of state to rebuild trust in elections and to make Nevada a better place to start a business. He says he would require voter identification and proof of citizenship, replace voting machines with precinct hand counts of paper ballots, and end universal mail ballots while keeping absentee voting for military, traveling, elderly, and medically unable voters. He says every voter should re-register and that Nevada should leave the Electronic Registration Information Center. He says he would advocate repeal of the commerce tax and lower fees to form a business.

Governor of Nebraska. His campaign says he is back at work after a horseback accident and that the next stretch is about commonsense conservative solutions. He says the state's overall tax burden is lower than when he took office. He says the next term should keep a focus on protecting children. He says he will promote Nebraska agriculture and defend what he calls Nebraska values. He says he will keep leading efforts to fix property taxes.

U.S. senator from Idaho seeking another term. He is a small-business owner, a farmer and beef producer, and a former county prosecuting attorney. He says that as governor he cut property taxes by 20 percent, and that he is a former chairman of the Senate Small Business Committee. He says he led the Senate fight against selling some of Idaho's public lands and will keep defending multiple use, including hunting, logging, and grazing. He says he will keep cutting taxes and red tape for small businesses and farms, and he cites a 100 percent approval rating from the American Farm Bureau. He says he supports border enforcement, Second Amendment rights, and returning natural-resource decisions to state and local leaders.

Broadcaster and Republican nominee for Florida's 19th District His campaign says he was born at Naples Community Hospital, married his high-school sweetheart, Carly, and raised their children in Southwest Florida. He earned a finance degree at Stetson, worked in Senator Connie Mack's Washington office in 1996, and runs Sun Broadcasting, including 92.5 FOX News Radio. He says he would stand with President Trump to secure the border, enforce immigration laws, and deport people who are here illegally. He says families are paying too much for groceries, housing, and insurance, and he would fight to bring those costs down. He says he would vote to make President Trump's tax cuts permanent so families and small businesses keep more of what they earn.

U.S. representative and former union organizer running for another term. Jimmy Gomez's campaign says he is the son of Mexican immigrants, grew up without health insurance, and worked his way from community college to UCLA and a public-policy degree at Harvard. It says he organized with a public-employee union and a nurses' union, served in the Assembly, and was elected to Congress in 2017. He says he is fighting for Medicare for All so a medical bill does not bankrupt a family. He says he championed an expansion of paid family leave in the Assembly and wants a national paid-family-leave program. He says he voted for the Inflation Reduction Act and has worked to lower prescription prices for seniors.

U.S. representative running for another term. Jimmy Panetta's campaign says he was elected to the House in 2016 and began as a prosecutor in the Alameda County District Attorney's Office in 1996. It says he serves on Ways and Means and the Budget Committee. He says he would ease inflation by investing in roads, rail, research, manufacturing, broadband, and water, and by expanding child care and equal pay. He says he has written bills to block offshore oil drilling, cut carbon emissions, and fund wildfire prevention and reforestation. He says he has pushed housing tax credits for low- and middle-income homes and grants for veterans and people who are homeless.

U.S. representative running for another term. Jimmy Patronis's campaign says he is a fourth-generation Floridian from Panama City who worked in his family's seafood restaurant, served eight years in the Florida House, and was the state's chief financial officer and fire marshal before winning a House seat. He says his House priorities follow an America First agenda: cutting taxes, restraining spending, investing in the military, and reforming veterans' services. He says that as chief financial officer he pushed benefits for firefighters diagnosed with cancer and mental-health care for first responders. He says he fought insurance practices that let contractors take over homeowners' benefits after storms and drive premiums up.

Retired Marine running for Congress in Arizona's 6th District. Her campaign says she is a working mother and retired Marine, the daughter of farmworkers who grew up in rural poverty. She says she is not a politician and has no tolerance for corruption. She says she would crack down on price gouging, modernize the child tax credit, oppose tariffs that raise costs, and strengthen Social Security. She says she would reverse health-care cuts, protect people with preexisting conditions, and expand Medicare drug-price negotiation. She says she would fund police, deport people who commit violent crimes, create a path to citizenship for people who follow the law, and require data centers to bring their own power.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

U.S. representative and former Texas state legislator from San Antonio. His official biography says he was born in San Antonio in 1974, raised on the West Side, and is a product of public schools. He graduated from Stanford and Harvard Law, served five terms in the Texas House, and was elected to Congress in 2012. He says he wants to build what he calls an infrastructure of opportunity: strong public schools and universities, a sound health-care system, and good jobs. His biography says that as a state legislator he helped restore funding for health care and education and worked on mental health, teen pregnancy, and juvenile justice. He says he created a college tour for students with few resources and founded SA READS, a San Antonio literacy campaign.

Milwaukee alder and former state representative running for secretary of state. Her campaign says she was born and raised on Milwaukee's south side, served ten years in the Assembly, and is in her second term on the Common Council. It says she was the first Latina and the first openly bisexual member of both bodies. She is using the campaign to call for state investment in affordable child care, housing, and relief on grocery costs. She says the secretary of state sits on the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands and that she would protect the trust funds and land that support public schools and libraries. She says she would push the state to fund public schools so districts rely less on local referenda.

Michigan secretary of state, running for governor. Jocelyn Benson's campaign says she is the daughter of two special-education teachers and, at 35, became the youngest woman to lead an accredited American law school as dean at Wayne State. She says she has been secretary of state since 2019 and is running so children, parents, and older residents can afford to stay. She says she would expand rural health-care options and build more housing. She says she would take on utility companies over the rates they charge. She says she would make child care free so more people can afford to live in the state.

Former assistant attorney general and prosecutor. Her campaign says she spent five years as an assistant attorney general in the consumer-protection bureau and was a deputy county attorney in Dawson and Dodge counties. She says she is running to return the office to serving Nebraskans rather than political fights. She says the attorney general should protect consumers rather than large corporations. She says enforcement should be both strong and fair so public safety and fairness go together. She says the office should respect the will of voters instead of fighting them each election cycle.

U.S. representative for Connecticut's 2nd District The campaign says Joe Courtney, a Connecticut native and lawyer, was elected to the U.S. House in 2006 after serving in the state House and as Vernon's town attorney. He chairs the Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee, which oversees submarine and ship construction. He says his first fight in Congress was to keep Electric Boat building submarines, and he still focuses on the shipyard and the region's defense work. He says he has worked to lower college costs, expand vocational programs, support farmers and veterans, and end surprise medical bills. His priorities page also lists infrastructure, agriculture, health care, and education.
District 11 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Republican

Mayor of Randolph running for Congress in New Jersey's 11th District. His campaign says he grew up in a middle-class family in Clifton, played football at Yale, and worked in government and corporate communications, including as an aide to former Governor Chris Christie. He says he joined the Randolph council in 2022, became mayor in 2025, and lives there with his wife and three children. He says he would cut taxes for first-time homebuyers, including a tax freeze and a refundable credit for closing costs. He says he would cap federal student-loan interest rather than cancel debt outright, and invest in vocational and technical training. He says he would expand the child tax credit and childcare tax relief, require upfront health-care prices, and finish the Gateway Tunnel.

Nevada's governor, running for another term. Joe Lombardo's campaign says he grew up in a military family, graduated from Rancho High School and UNLV, served in the Army and the Nevada National Guard, and spent 26 years with the Las Vegas police before two terms as Clark County sheriff. He says that as governor he has cut regulation, made large investments in education, and pushed accountability in schools. He says he has backed law enforcement and worked on the housing shortage. He says the unfinished work is a safer, stronger, and more prosperous state.

Marine veteran and city council member running for Congress. Joe Males's campaign says he enlisted in the Marines after turning 18, served in the Philippines and Guam, and later built a computer-networking business. It says he is a Hemet council member and a father. He says he ran for council after his son, also a Marine, was murdered, because he wants the rule of law so other families do not face that loss. He says his council work has focused on infrastructure, business growth, and safer, cleaner neighborhoods. He says he would bring that same results-focused approach to Washington for the Inland Empire and Imperial County.

Former Iowa legislator and housing developer running for Congress. Born and raised south of Cedar Rapids, he says he was sworn into the Iowa House at 21, the youngest state legislator in state history, and later worked on housing at HUD and the Federal Housing Finance Agency. He develops workforce housing in rural Iowa and says younger Iowans should be able to afford to stay. He says he takes no corporate PAC money and supports term limits of 12 years in the House and 12 in the Senate, plus a ban on members of Congress trading stocks. He says immigration policy should put Americans first, including a secure border, removal of people he describes as criminal illegal immigrants, and a temporary ban on H-1B visas. He says deregulating homebuilding would lower home prices, and he wants lower taxes for middle-class families and small businesses and fewer rules on farmers.

U.S. representative for Colorado's 2nd District. Joe Neguse's campaign says he represents the 2nd District and is the first African American elected to Congress from Colorado. It says his parents came to the United States as refugees from Eritrea, and that before Congress he was a lawyer, a CU regent, and head of the state's consumer-protection agency. He says public lands are central to the district, and that he moved a Colorado public-lands bill through the House that would preserve about 400,000 acres and has pushed money toward wildfire preparation. He says climate change is an existential threat, and that he has pressed for more solar power, renewable energy, and deep cuts in carbon emissions. He says health coverage should be available to everyone, and that he is working to lower drug prices, raise the minimum wage, and close the gender pay gap.

Businessman and Republican nominee for Florida's 11th District His campaign says he started as a high-school handyman, entered the skilled trades, and grew a family-owned Central Florida company, Strada Services, that created thousands of jobs and paid training pathways. He and his wife raised their family in Central Florida. He says he is a father and grandfather running as an outsider, not for a career in politics. He says he would investigate congressional insider trading, enact term limits, and pass a balanced-budget amendment. He says he would finish the border wall, back law enforcement, and cut waste before asking taxpayers for more. He says he would lower costs, restore energy independence, bring jobs back, and protect Social Security and Medicare.

Youth worker and community organizer running for the U.S. Senate. Joe Tache's site says he is a socialist based in Boston who has spent more than ten years in movements against worker exploitation, war, police brutality, and gentrification, and that he writes and teaches that capitalism is the root of those problems. He says the largest corporations should be taken into public control and the economy reorganized around housing, health care, food, education, child care, retirement, and a living wage. He says climate policy and meaningful jobs require working people in power, and he wants spending shifted from war to domestic needs. He says immigrants, Black Americans, women, and LGBTQ people should not be blamed for the crisis, and he wants rent capped as a share of income, free health care, and millions of union jobs.
District 2 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Republican

U.S. representative who chairs the Armed Services Readiness Subcommittee. His campaign says he is a veteran leader in Congress who serves on Armed Services, Foreign Affairs, and Education and the Workforce, and as an assistant majority whip. He says he is committed to conservative values and works to enact the Trump agenda. He says he promotes a strong national defense and peace through strength. He says he is working to create jobs and to limit the size and scope of the federal government. He says his commitments also cover the economy and veterans' services.
District 9 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Brooklyn small-business owner running for Congress in New York's 9th District. His campaign says he is a small businessman in Brooklyn who also coaches men's volleyball at Brooklyn College. It says he graduated from Union College in 2005 with a degree in civil engineering. He says the country should bring manufacturing home and stay out of a major war so it can reinvest in infrastructure, pointing to tensions over Taiwan and Greenland. He warns that artificial intelligence could outrun human guardrails and asks how government stays accountable if machines run more of the market and the state.

Connecticut attorney and former Westport planning and zoning commissioner He says he is a Connecticut attorney and a former member of the Westport Planning and Zoning Commission. He says he grew up as the son of a longtime auditor in the Connecticut State Auditors of Public Accounts. He says he would make utility rate cases a priority and challenge policies that raise electric costs. He says he would investigate AI-driven pricing and pursue consumer fraud, including scams aimed at seniors. He says he would hold neighboring states accountable when pollution harms Connecticut rivers, drinking water, or Long Island Sound.

Navy veteran and small-business owner running for Congress. He calls himself a citizen-legislator who has balanced budgets, signed paychecks, and fought to put parents in control of schools. He wants spending that feeds inflation cut back, and less red tape for small manufacturers and the skilled trades. He supports a federal parents' bill of rights, lower public-university tuition, and more training in the trades. He says he would shut down open-air drug markets, interdict fentanyl, finish border barriers, and continue sea-lion control to help salmon runs.

U.S. representative running for another term. John Carter's campaign says he settled in Central Texas with his wife after law degrees from Texas Tech and the University of Texas, practiced in Round Rock, and was appointed a Williamson County district judge before Congress. His issues page lists border security, protecting the homeland, care for veterans, lower taxes and a stronger economy, the Second Amendment, and protecting children. He says he treats Central Texas as home and comes back after votes rather than staying in Washington.

Neurosurgeon and small-business owner running for Congress. He says his family has been in Bartow County since the 1930s, that he grew up on the family farm, graduated from Cartersville High School, and has cared for patients across the 11th District for decades. He and his wife, Dr. Anne Cowan, are raising four children, and he says he serves as a church elder. U.S. representative and former state legislator running for another term. Juan Vargas's campaign says he was born in National City to Mexican immigrant parents who raised ten children on a chicken ranch. It says he earned degrees from the University of San Diego, Fordham, and Harvard Law, worked with the Jesuits in El Salvador, and served on the city council, in the Legislature, and in Congress. He says he is working to grow good-paying jobs through clean energy, infrastructure, and small businesses. He says he has championed public education and services for communities that have been left out. His site says he is also fighting to protect health care and veterans.

U.S. representative running for another term. Judy Chu's campaign says she was elected to the House in 2009 and represents Pasadena and the west San Gabriel Valley. It says she serves on Ways and Means and the Budget Committee and is chair emerita of the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus. She says her Ways and Means work covers taxes, trade, Social Security, and Medicare, including health care and safety-net programs. She says the caucus she led expanded language access in federal agencies and pushed for data that reflects Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities. She says she co-chairs a bipartisan caucus on creative rights.

U.S. representative from Louisiana running for the Senate. Julia Letlow's site says she is a Louisiana native, mother, and educator who entered Congress after her husband, Luke, died, and that she was the first Republican woman elected to Congress from Louisiana. She says her work in Congress has been for parents, students, farmers, law enforcement, and Louisiana families. She says she is guided by faith, family, service, and love of the state. She says she is running for the Senate to give Louisiana conservative leadership, and she notes President Trump's endorsement.

Lieutenant governor since 2019 · former state representative · won the primary with 40.4% South Side of Chicago. Daughter of a Navy veteran and a Chicago public-school teacher, and a mother of four. She finished ahead of Raja Krishnamoorthi and Robin Kelly, and she is not taking corporate PAC money in this race. $25 federal minimum wage, a larger earned-income credit and child tax credit, and a middle-class tax cut paid for by higher taxes on income above $1 million. Medicare for All, including home care, hearing, and vision. She opposes the current tariffs, which she calls a tax on groceries and goods. Restore Roe-level abortion protections, pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Act and gun laws, and abolish ICE. Her housing plan targets hedge-fund home purchases and algorithm-set rents.
District 1 · U.S. House · North Dakota · Republican

Candidate for Congress The campaign says Julie Fedorchak is a fourth-generation North Dakotan, born in Williston and a University of North Dakota graduate, who later ran a communications business and served on the Public Service Commission. She says she is running to be a practical voice for the state's energy and farm economy. She says that on the Public Service Commission she pushed to finish the Dakota Access Pipeline and to keep coal and oil energy reliable and affordable. Her issues list includes securing the border, reducing the federal debt, backing law enforcement, and defending the Second Amendment. She says she will work with President Trump to secure North Dakota's energy and agricultural future and to support farmers and ranchers.

Community finance executive running for Oakland mayor. Julius Robinson says he grew up in Watts and has spent more than four decades connecting capital, opportunity, and communities. He says he is running because Oakland needs practical results on safety, housing, and trust in City Hall. He says the city should be safer and cleaner, and that businesses need support to grow. He says housing, homelessness, and economic opportunity have to be handled together. He says local government should operate with more transparency and accountability.

Peace and Justice Party candidate for governor of Vermont. Her campaign says the major parties maintain economic and environmental injustice, and that her platform is a just and inclusive society with wealth and power shared more equally. She wants profitable businesses to pay a living wage and wants Vermont's universal health care law fully carried out. She proposes progressive taxes, including higher taxes on high incomes and on buildings left vacant most of the year, in place of homestead taxes for education. She wants community hubs where people can offer skills and get help, plus housing support such as cooperative ownership and no-interest mortgages for modest homes.
