Army veteran running for Congress. Justin Early's campaign says he is a Georgetown father of seven and a cybersecurity architect at Dell whose parents served in the Army. It says he enlisted after Leander High School, served as a paratrooper, and worked at the Defense Intelligence Agency. He says his priorities are affordability, responsible technology and AI, and defending democracy. He says families are squeezed by the cost of living and unaffordable health care, and that he is not a career politician.

Republican candidate for U.S. Senate. Justin Murphy is the Republican nominee. His campaign says it is dedicated to members of the armed forces and publishes a written pledge of his positions. He says he wants the Pinelands kept intact and the Jersey Shore kept free of pollution and offshore wind turbines. He lists parental rights, medical freedom, and Medicare for seniors among his national priorities. He says he would argue conservative positions and calls the race a break from a long stretch without a Republican senator from New Jersey.

State representative running for Congress in Tennessee's 9th District. His campaign says he is the fourth of five sons of teenage parents in Memphis, and that his parents worked their way through college and out of poverty. He says he is a state representative who was expelled after a protest, then reappointed and reelected, and that he is married to Oceana R. Gilliam. He says he would guarantee jobs, raise the minimum wage to a living wage, pass the PRO Act, and make billionaires and large corporations pay more. He supports Medicare for All, rural hospitals, and the veterans' health system, and he wants permits to carry, a ban on assault rifles, and background checks. He says he would pause large data-center construction, overturn Citizens United, and ban members of Congress from trading stock.

Veteran and engineer running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 16th District. Justin Wagner was born and raised in Greenville and Transfer and says his family has lived there for eight generations. He describes himself as a veteran, engineer, and pro-union candidate running for safer and more self-reliant communities. He says housing, health care, power, and food costs are pushing working families into poverty, and that he would fight for affordability, local veterans, and labor. He also says every school needs the tools to prepare the next generation, the justice system should be fair, and the environment should stay safe for future children.
District 22 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Former Agriculture Department chief of staff running for Congress in New York's 22nd District. Her campaign says she grew up in Auburn in a blue-collar family, was the first in her family to finish college, and most recently was chief of staff to the secretary of agriculture. It says she is a working mother of three running to lower costs for Central New York. She says she would grow good-paying jobs and lower everyday costs so families do not have to leave New York to get ahead. She says her work in government has focused on cutting red tape, strengthening American agriculture, and protecting jobs in the food and energy supply chain.

Mayor of Los Angeles running for re-election. Karen Bass is campaigning for another term as mayor. Her campaign page says she is standing up for Angelenos against federal immigration raids. She says the Trump administration's ICE raids and militarized actions have no purpose other than to create fear. She says those actions damage the city's economy and tear families apart.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Educator, author, and Libertarian candidate for U.S. Senate Kasie Whitener's campaign describes her as a community leader, author, educator, and radio personality. She says she would be an independent vote in the Senate rather than a party operative. She says she would simplify the tax code, return to actual budgets, and cut federal spending across agencies. She says she would separate health insurance from employment and remove barriers that keep people from starting medical practices. She says she wants a balanced-budget amendment, no new foreign wars, and no new federal abortion laws or new limits on the Second Amendment.

U.S. representative running for another term. Kat Cammack's campaign says she is in her third term from Florida's 3rd District. It says she and her husband, a Gainesville firefighter and paramedic, are raising their daughter in North Central Florida. She says she is focused on securing the southern border, advocating for small businesses, and defending the Second Amendment. She describes herself as a budget hawk who wants taxes low and federal spending kept minimal.

House Democratic whip representing Massachusetts' 5th District. She says she first ran in 2013 because of the issues facing women, children, and families, and that colleagues elected her Democratic whip in 2022, the highest-ranking woman from Massachusetts in House history. She says the people of the district are why she is running again. She says she is fighting to cancel cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act, end a war she says raised gas prices, and lift tariffs that made goods more expensive. She says that if Democrats control Congress she would lead efforts to crack down on ICE, stop unauthorized wars, and hold the president accountable for using the office to enrich himself. She says every worker should have a living wage, paid family leave, and the right to join a union, and she highlights the expanded child tax credit in the American Rescue Plan.

Chief counsel to the Alabama attorney general Katherine Robertson is a graduate of Auburn University and the University of Alabama School of Law and has been chief counsel to Attorney General Steve Marshall for nearly a decade. She previously was vice president of the Alabama Policy Institute and worked in Washington as clerk and counsel to Senator Jeff Sessions. She says her work has been to fight what she calls federal overreach. She says she has fought efforts she describes as attacks on women's sports, free speech, and the sanctity of life. She says she is running to defend the rights and freedoms of Alabamians.

U.S. representative running for another term. Kathy Castor's campaign says she is a native Floridian and the first woman elected to represent Hillsborough and Pinellas counties in Congress. It says she was a lawyer and Hillsborough County commissioner before joining the House Energy and Commerce Committee. She says she works to lower family costs, create jobs, and protect Florida's environment, including wetlands and the coast. She says she helped pass the bipartisan infrastructure law, bills expanding care for seriously ill children, and veterans' caucus work.

Governor of New York, seeking another term. Her campaign calls her New York's first mom governor and says she has focused on putting money back in people's pockets, lowering costs, and keeping New Yorkers safe. She is running with New York City Council Speaker Adrienne Adams. She points to inflation refund checks, a larger child tax credit, middle-class tax cuts, and work toward universal child care and lower auto insurance costs. She highlights free school meals, a ban on cell phones during the school day, and gun laws she says are meant to make streets and subways safer. She says the ticket would keep lowering costs, invest in community safety, and protect New York from what she calls MAGA extremism.

Attorney General of Delaware She says she was born and raised in Wilmington, graduated from the University of Delaware and Villanova University Law School, and started as a prosecutor in the Delaware Department of Justice. She says she later served as state prosecutor and chief deputy attorney general before returning to lead the office. She says she is running to make Delaware safer and to make justice fair and equal. She says she prosecuted domestic violence, sexual assault, and homicide cases, and that she built the office's consumer-fraud work. She says that as attorney general she has pursued child predators, opioid manufacturers, corruption, and elder abuse, and is pushing stronger laws on online predators.

Governor of Arizona Katie Hobbs is a social worker who was elected Arizona secretary of state and then governor, taking office in 2022. Her campaign says that before politics she worked with homeless youth and helped run a large domestic-violence shelter. She says she eliminated the tax on rent, offered down-payment help for first homes, and cut red tape to make housing more affordable. She says she created a Border Coordination Office, sent more than $100 million in border-security funding to local police, and that Task Force SAFE has stopped over 19 million fentanyl pills. She says a water compromise passed under her watch will create jobs, lower housing costs, and conserve water, and that she ended a foreign corporation's groundwater leases.

Teacher and attorney running for Congress. Katy Padilla Stout's campaign says she was born and raised in South Texas, taught school, and worked as an attorney for children in foster care. It says she and her husband are raising four children and she is running to be the first woman to represent the 23rd District. She says the cost of living comes from the current administration's economic policies, and that the tax code should help the middle class rather than cut taxes for billionaires while food aid is debated. She says she would expand Medicare toward coverage for everyone and treat gun ownership as a right that still allows commonsense limits.

Attorney and business owner running for Congress. Katy Tyndell's site says she is an attorney and business owner whose family roots in Kansas go back five generations, and that she grew up in a small ranching and farming town. It says she was a staff attorney for the National Congress of American Indians and later co-founded Leading Kansas. She says she will work for affordable health care, including mental health care, after her family navigated a sister's schizophrenia and she watched insurance premiums rise at her business. She says she will look for common ground to lower taxes on working Kansans and bring costs down, instead of tax breaks aimed at corporations and the wealthy. She says tariffs and the war with Iran have hurt Kansas farm markets and raised fertilizer and diesel costs, and that she will fight to reverse those tariff policies and end the war.

Working mother and organizer running for Idaho's 1st District. Her campaign says she is a 36-year-old working mother and a sixth-generation Idahoan. She says she has spent nearly five years, across three election cycles, organizing in a district she describes as about 500 miles long. She says she takes no corporate PAC money, would ban stock trades by members of Congress and their families, and supports term limits of six House terms and two Senate terms. She says she would cut taxes on middle-class families and local businesses, raise the federal minimum wage, repeal right-to-work laws, and direct USDA help to family farms. She says Idaho's public lands are not for sale, and she would fund the Forest Service, local timber, and wildfire work, and move health coverage to a universal single-payer system.

Former Atlanta mayor running for governor. She was Atlanta's 60th mayor and says she is the first mayor in the city's history to have served in all three branches of city government, as a judge, a city council member, and mayor. She says the city balanced four budgets without a property-tax increase, layoffs, or furloughs, and that reserves stood near $181 million at the end of her term. She says that as mayor she secured major investments in affordable housing and a historic pay raise for Atlanta's first responders. She says she supported small businesses and became a national voice on civil-rights reforms. She says the city balanced its budgets through a downturn without property-tax increases, layoffs, or furloughs.

Attorney general of Minnesota. His campaign says Minnesotans first elected him attorney general in 2018 and that he calls the job the people's lawyer. The site says the office has gone after insulin prices, opioid companies, scams, and medical debt. He says the office has lowered costs, including cutting the price of insulin, and has taken on price-gouging, medical debt, and opioid companies. He says he is protecting tenants, going after scammers, and standing up for student borrowers. He says he is challenging the Trump administration because no one is above the law, and that he is defending reproductive rights and access to gender-affirming care.

Ohio auditor of state running for attorney general. His campaign says he was elected auditor after more than two decades that included private-sector work and public office, and that he keeps a law practice in Celina. It says his audit team has pursued criminal cases against public officials and findings to recover taxpayer money. He says he would defend constitutional rights, including religious liberty, and challenge federal actions he argues exceed federal authority. He says he would fight the drug epidemic with treatment, prosecutions, and efforts to cut supply chains, and that he would work with police on human trafficking and survivor services. He says he would enforce consumer-protection laws against fraud, scams, and deceptive businesses, especially cases that target seniors, and he proposes a program to help patients challenge health-insurance denials.

U.S. representative running for another term. Keith Self's campaign says he is a native Texan, West Point graduate, and retired Army lieutenant colonel who served in the infantry and Special Forces. It says that after the Army he was Collin County judge and is seeking another term in Congress. He says he voted to restart border-wall construction, offered a bill to use seized cartel money on border security, and wants the federal government to repay Texas for its border spending. He says he cut the county property-tax rate, opposes stopgap federal budgets, and wants lower taxes, less spending, and energy permitting that expands American production. He says he started a caucus to stop what he calls the spread of Sharia law in Texas and the country.

Candidate for U.S. House in Colorado's 2nd District. Kelley Dennison says she is a Colorado native with roots in mountain towns and the Front Range, and a business owner. She says she is running so those communities have a voice in Congress on costs, energy, and the state's land and water. She says families are squeezed by housing, gas, inflation, and property taxes, and that the district should do better by veterans and seniors. She says parents should be partners in their children's education, and that responsible gun owners should not be punished for crimes committed by other people. She says she has signed a pledge to cosponsor and vote for a constitutional amendment limiting how long any person can serve in Congress.
District 1 · U.S. House · Rhode Island · Republican

Republican candidate and public-health worker running for Congress. Her campaign says she was born and raised in Boston, is a mother of three daughters, attended Boston Latin School and Suffolk University, and served in AmeriCorps. She says her career began at the nation's first community health center and grew into public-health operations. She says she would lower everyday costs and energy bills, offer tax relief for working families and seniors, and make housing more affordable. She says she would cut red tape for small businesses, expand workforce training, invest in community health centers, and support the ocean economy. She says she supports a parental bill of rights, curriculum transparency, school choice, stronger public safety, and secure borders.

New Hampshire's governor, running for another term. Kelly Ayotte is the state's 83rd governor. Her campaign says she previously served as attorney general and as a U.S. senator, and that she lives in Nashua. She says her first term sped up housing construction, fully funded child-care scholarships, and produced a balanced budget with no new taxes. She says she got cell phones out of classrooms, raised per-student school funding, and put more weight on reading. She says she rewrote bail rules, strengthened laws on domestic violence and trafficking, and used her veto on bills she calls hidden sales taxes.

Navy veteran and small-business CFO running for Georgia's 8th District. His campaign says he served from 1999 to 2002 as a nuclear operator on the USS Henry M. Jackson, and that he was the first Black nuclear operator on that boat during his service. He earned a PhD in public policy from Walden University and is chief financial officer of BroTagz Embroidery. He says he served on the Hapeville zoning board, as a legislative aide to State Senator Donzella James, and on the effort that created the city of South Fulton. He says education is a public good and he would fund affordable learning beyond K-12, including job skills for the district's health-care, retail, and manufacturing workers. He says he would strengthen Medicaid, Medicare, and VA care and fund rural clinics and hospitals, in a district he ties to Robins Air Force Base. He says he would seek federal money for roads, broadband, and utility upgrades, including solar and wind where communities want them, and back labor standards for workers.

Educator and consultant running for lieutenant governor. His campaign says he is a lifelong Oklahoman raised in Skiatook and Broken Arrow, the first in his family to graduate from college, and the holder of a doctorate in administration and leadership. It says he has taught and administered schools, owns Kelly B's Consulting, and serves on the board of Oklahoma City's family justice center. He says he would invest in small business, CareerTech, workforce training, and partnerships with Native nations, and would work on affordable housing and food insecurity. He says he would put more funding into public schools, respect teachers, and keep public dollars in public schools. He says he would expand health-care access in underserved places, promote tourism, and lead the office with public integrity rather than as a career politician.

Longtime manager of teams and operations Kelly Grappe says she spent decades leading teams, managing complex systems, and serving customers and businesses, and that she is not running because she has had a career in politics. She says she is running for secretary of state to take politics out of the office and make it work for the public. She says she will show how votes are cast, protected, counted, and verified, and answer doubts with facts rather than dismiss them. She says she will defend Arkansas's authority to run its own elections and oppose efforts to nationalize that work. She says transparency is one of the ways to build confidence that elections are secure.

Former Sarasota mayor and Democratic nominee for Florida's 16th District His campaign says he is a third-generation Floridian and a single father who grew up working his family's citrus stand near the Sarasota-Bradenton airport. He earned bachelor's and master's degrees from Georgetown, then spent four years in the Peace Corps in northern Guatemala. He later served as a Sarasota commissioner and mayor, built a nonprofit that helped first-generation students reach college without debt, and was a vice president at Eckerd College. He says he would lower insurance, health-care, and prescription costs, restore Medicare and Medicaid funding, and let the government negotiate drug prices. He says he would expand affordable housing and stop Wall Street from buying single-family homes. He says he would protect Tampa Bay, Sarasota Bay, and the coast by prohibiting offshore drilling and enforcing the Clean Water Act.

U.S. representative and OB-GYN. Kelly Morrison's campaign says she is a sixth-generation Minnesotan who practiced as an OB-GYN for more than 20 years and is the first pro-choice OB-GYN elected to Congress. She says she grew up and raised three children in the west metro, and that her husband John is an Army combat veteran. She says she is fighting health-care cuts she says would push Minnesotans off insurance and force hospitals to close, and that no one should go bankrupt to get care. She says she is working to exempt small businesses from tariffs and get them refunds, and to lower the costs of housing and child care. She says she takes no corporate PAC, federal-lobbyist, or dark-money money, supports a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United, and backs a ban on stock ownership by presidents, vice presidents, and members of Congress.

Mother, concrete-business owner, and nonprofit founder running for Congress. She says she is a mother of six and grandmother of 12, married to her high school sweetheart, with a business degree from the University of Central Florida. She co-owns a concrete contracting company serving northern Indiana and founded a nonprofit for at-risk youth. She says she would lower costs for housing, health care, education, utilities, and energy, and fight for Medicare for All. She says she would fully fund education from child care to college by taxing Wall Street, and put Hoosiers ahead of corporations and foreign governments. She says she would end U.S. wars in the Middle East and bring troops home, ban stock trading by Congress and the president, and release the Epstein files.

U.S. representative running in a newly drawn district. Ken Calvert's campaign says he is a lifelong Corona resident and a former small-business owner who now chairs the Defense Appropriations Subcommittee. It says that after Proposition 50 he is running in the 40th District, where Corona is the largest city. He says he wrote the law that created E-Verify and wants employers required to use it. He says he has secured more than a billion dollars for transportation, water, and clean-air projects in Riverside County. He says his office has helped veterans and seniors get benefits they are owed.

Information technology entrepreneur and Libertarian candidate for governor Ken Krawchuk's campaign says he has been a registered Libertarian since 1993 and is running for governor with John Thomas for lieutenant governor. The site says he was born in Philadelphia's Feltonville section and has lived in Abington for decades. He says he would veto tax increases, use the line-item veto, phase out the personal income tax, and abolish property taxes. He says he would end the state's monopoly on schooling and privatize public schools because too many students are behind in reading and math. His listed program also says he would eliminate parole for violent criminals, pardon nonviolent drug offenders, and decriminalize marijuana.

Candidate for the U.S. Senate. His campaign calls him a former attorney general who fought federal policies in court and is now running for the Senate. He says he will carry the president's agenda in Washington. He says he will push tax cuts, border security, deportations, an end to what he calls the weaponization of government, and less federal spending. He says he will take on large drug and food companies, seek more transparency in food and health care, and side with a Make America Healthy Again effort. He says he will defend gun rights and laws against abortion, oppose transgender participation in girls' sports, and support a clear legal framework for crypto, including the CLARITY Act.

Independent candidate for governor Kenneth Block is running for governor as an independent. His site says he wants the state government held accountable for waste, failed projects, and rising taxes. He says the state budget is about $15 billion and that residents are not getting services that match what they pay. He points to the Washington Bridge and large technology projects as examples of agencies repeating mistakes. He says his focus is accountability, fixing broken processes, and results for residents.

Third-generation Wyomingite and Vietnam veteran running for governor. He told Wyoming Public Media he was born in Cheyenne in 1950, that his family has worked in Wyoming for three generations, and that he ran a small business in Elk Mountain for 28 years. He does not have a campaign website. He says his first issue is free and open elections: a person should be able to file and run without having to join a party. He says health care is the main reason young people leave, and he wants a statewide system that connects rural clinics. He says he wants small business to grow, and he wants property tax ended for people once they turn 65.

Mechanical engineer running for Utah's 3rd District. He was born in Lehi, worked with mining, petroleum, geothermal, and solar industries, and says much of his career was spent on water, environmental cleanup, and teaching engineers. He says he is running because Washington has grown more divisive and disconnected, and he wants a representative who honors the Constitution. He calls for a moratorium on new data centers and says his priorities include Utah's land and water, Social Security, and the cost of health care. He says he takes no corporate PAC money and has pledged to limit his own term.

Marine veteran running for Congress. Kevin Burge's campaign says he is a Marine veteran with more than 20 years of leadership and deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he grew up without wealth in Los Alamos. It says his wife immigrated from Honduras, serves in the Texas Army National Guard, and their son attends public school in Tarrant County. He says he would fast-track affordable housing, crack down on corporate landlords, raise the minimum wage, and expand Medicaid. He says he supports Medicare for All, restoring abortion rights, tuition-free public college, and rules so data centers recycle water and limit pollution.

Candidate for U.S. Senate who says he was born on an Air Force base. His campaign says he earned an architectural drafting certificate in high school, used it to pay for an engineering degree, and later earned an MBA. It says that in office he has backed the Trump administration's agenda. He says he has backed bills to recognize groups of veterans and a constitutional amendment aimed at a balanced budget. He says he has voted to fund a border wall and to cut off federal money for sanctuary campuses, and that he wants small businesses to get capital. He says he would protect religious liberty, restrict abortion funding, and protect gun rights, including concealed-carry reciprocity.

Independent U.S. representative running for another term. Kevin Kiley's campaign says he grew up in the communities of the new 6th District, taught high school English, and prosecuted cases as a deputy attorney general before serving in the Assembly and winning a House seat in 2022. It says he chairs the subcommittee covering K-12 education and child care. He says he has worked across parties on measures to lower the cost of gasoline, groceries, utilities, and insurance. He points to a federal grant to ease traffic near Highways 65 and 80 and to a Lake Tahoe restoration law he says funds wildfire mitigation. He says he helped restore Medicare funding for senior programs and is focused on prosecuting violent crime and protecting children from fentanyl.

Former Stockton mayor and Marine veteran running for Congress. Kevin Lincoln's campaign says he was born in Stockton, raised in a military family, and joined the Marines in 2001, later serving on Marine One. It says he then managed a private-security district in Silicon Valley, became a Stockton pastor, and was elected mayor in 2019. He says he would secure the border, enforce immigration laws, and treat fentanyl trafficking as a threat to Valley families. He says he would cut wasteful spending and lower taxes as grocery, gas, and rent costs climb, pointing to budgets he balanced as mayor without a tax increase. He says he would oppose early release and shorter sentences for repeat offenders, and he highlights police pay and budget increases he backed as mayor.

Corporate controller running for Congress in Georgia's 6th District. He says he has spent 30 years as a controller, the person who audits the books, and that he is a fifth-generation native of Cobb County who has lived in the district his whole life. He says voters should be in charge of the people they elect. On schools, he wants federal education money returned to Georgia without federal strings, and he wants student aid and career programs to cover shorter technical training. On the budget, he says Congress should pass a budget through regular order, fund core obligations first, and make every other program justify another appropriation. He also says law enforcement should be funded, federal law should focus on people who have done something, there should be no national gun registry, and defense spending should start from readiness and replenishment rather than the size of the check.

Green Party candidate for lieutenant governor. He says he is the Green Party candidate and that the campaign will depend on voters telling other people, because he expects little corporate-media coverage. He says the lieutenant governor should judge bills by whether they protect health and a decent life for every Texan. He says his first bills would expand city bus fleets, invest in rural family-farm greenhouses and hemp, and change elections to ranked-choice voting, one statewide primary, and a nonpartisan redistricting commission. He says he would appraise property by rent or lease value instead of comparable sales and drop exemptions he calls special-interest favors. He says he favors a moratorium on data centers with strict limits on their electricity and water, and legal THC with rules to protect the public.

U.S. representative running for another term. Kevin Mullin's campaign says he was raised in South San Francisco, has lived on the Peninsula his whole life, and has been a local business owner and a D.J. It says he has served in local, state, and federal office and sits on the Energy and Commerce Committee. He says he would lower housing costs, send federal money to local child-care programs, and update the federal poverty line. He says he is defending medical research and the innovation economy in his district. His campaign also lists health-care costs, climate action, reproductive rights, and a fairer tax policy among his priorities.

Arkansas state senator and pastor Kim Hammer of Benton was elected to the state Senate in 2018 after eight years in the House, and he chairs the Senate Efficiency Committee. He has been pastor of Saline Missionary Baptist Church in Tull since 1978 and chaired the start of Saline Memorial Hospice. His campaign biography says that in the 94th General Assembly he sponsored bills to protect election integrity, including limits on electioneering near voting sites and authority for the legislature to look into voting irregularities. It says his priorities include making motor-vehicle registration and driver's-license renewal simpler. It says he was the lead sponsor of Act 403 of 2021, which lets the legislature end an executive order for a statewide public-health emergency.

Pediatrician and U.S. representative for Washington's 8th District. She chairs the Democratic Doctors Caucus and says travel around the district keeps turning up families squeezed by higher prices. She wrote a bill to suspend the federal gas tax for temporary relief, and she says she is fighting corporate price gouging, grocery mergers, and tariffs that hit farmers and small businesses. She is pushing housing bills, including a permanent housing-affordability proposal and support for the bipartisan Road to Housing package. She wants ACA premium tax credits restored and Republican Medicaid cuts undone so rural hospitals and Apple Health coverage stay in place.

Former prosecutor running for attorney general Kimberly Ahern's campaign says she was a prosecutor, advised two governors and three attorneys general, and worked as a regulator. It says she lives in Providence. She says that as attorney general she would put the criminal unit first and prosecute violent offenders, including murder, sexual assault, domestic violence, and trafficking. She says she would expand diversion so people with mental illness or addiction can get treatment while communities stay safe.

U.S. representative for Georgia's 6th District. She says the title that matters most is mom. After her son Jordan Davis was shot and killed in 2012, she left a 30-year career at Delta Air Lines, worked with Everytown for Gun Safety and Moms Demand Action, and then ran for the seat once held by Newt Gingrich. She highlights House passage of universal background checks and red-flag laws, and she says her work in Congress is aimed at laws that help children and families. A two-time breast cancer survivor, she says communities need affordable care, including cancer screening, contraceptives, and family-planning services, and she opposed defunding Planned Parenthood. She supports the Equality Act to bar LGBTQ discrimination in work, housing, and credit, and she points to federal infrastructure spending for safe water, high-speed internet, and a cleaner environment.

Former mayor of Hartford running for Congress The campaign says Luke Bronin was mayor of Hartford from 2016 to 2024, where he worked to pull the city back from bankruptcy, add housing, and create the Hartford Youth Service Corps. He says he is running because families are struggling while billionaires get tax breaks. He says he will focus on bringing down costs for housing, health care, groceries, childcare, and elder care. He wants Medicare and Medicaid protected and a push toward universal health care. He says he would abolish ICE, build more housing, and safeguard reproductive freedom.

Engineer and U.S. representative running for another term. Luz Rivas's campaign says she grew up in Pacoima with a single mother who had immigrated from Mexico, then earned an electrical-engineering degree from MIT and a master's in education from Harvard. It says she worked at Motorola, founded a girls' science nonprofit, served six years in the Assembly, and was elected to the House in 2025. She says her Assembly priority was funding for infrastructure, education, and health care in the Valley, along with environmental justice. She says she worked to expand computer-science and climate education across California. Her campaign says that in her first House term she joined Democratic leadership and co-chairs a bipartisan STEM education caucus.

Libertarian candidate for the U.S. Senate. Her campaign says she is from Ironwood in the Upper Peninsula, with a background in computer science, and that she built the campaign herself without PAC money. She says Michigan needs a senator who answers to residents rather than a political machine. She says she would protect the Great Lakes and push affordable health care, including Medicaid for all. She calls for fair wages, green jobs, and support for small businesses, and for social, racial, and LGBTQIA+ equity. She says she would defend voting rights and constitutional freedoms, and that she is not beholden to party bosses or corporate donors.

Former teacher running for governor. Her campaign says she is a lifelong Nebraskan, a former teacher, a mother, and a faith leader. She says she is running to bring what she calls common sense, compassion, and integrity back to the governor's office. She says she wants low taxes, strong schools, and an economy where people can get ahead. She says leaders should follow votes the public has already cast, including on medical marijuana, paid sick leave, the minimum wage, and school vouchers. She says she would push for a government that tells people what they need to know, not only what they want to hear.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 4th District. Madeleine Dean is a mother, grandmother, professor, and lawyer from Glenside who was first elected to Congress in 2018. Her campaign says she focuses on education, health care, gun violence, clean water, ethical government, and infrastructure. She says she will keep working to expand access to health care and to reduce gun violence. She also lists clean water and the climate, ethical governance, and infrastructure among her priorities.
District 2 · U.S. House · New Hampshire · Democratic

U.S. representative for New Hampshire's 2nd District The campaign says Maggie Goodlander grew up in Nashua, served more than a decade in the Navy Reserve, and later worked at the Justice Department and as a White House senior advisor. It says she is now in her first term in Congress. Her campaign says her priorities are lowering costs, taking on corruption that raises prices, and keeping promises to Americans. The site says that work includes housing bills meant to build more homes and limit corporate purchases of single-family houses, plus protections for Social Security and for veterans and military families. She says she has pushed to end emergency tariffs and to wind down U.S. hostilities with Iran.
