Council vote, added across the regions

Sacramento City Council member running for Congress. Mai Vang's campaign says she is the daughter of Hmong refugees, the oldest of 16 children, and the first in her family to attend college. It says she has been a teacher, a school board member, and a Sacramento City Council member focused on neighborhoods the city had overlooked. She says she takes no corporate PAC money and would raise the minimum wage with inflation, tax billionaires, and pass the PRO Act. She says she would fight for Medicare for All, an end to medical debt, and federal protection of reproductive care. She says she would fund more affordable housing, stop corporations from buying up single-family homes, and pause new data centers so households do not pay their power costs.
District 5 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Democratic

Campaign manager and candidate who says she puts people over party. Her campaign says she and her husband are raising children and that she has long supported nonpartisan advocacy and independent voters. She says that in 2022 she began managing campaigns and that in 2024 she helped seven candidates win in South Carolina. She says voters she met are unhappy with divisive politics, high costs, unreliable health care, attacks on public education, and congressional gridlock. She says she will fight for practical solutions through conversation and collaboration, and that she will not bend her values to party or special interests. She says she advocates legislation to make it easier for independents to vote and run for office.

Former state representative running for U.S. House in Colorado's 8th District. Manny Rutinel says he is the son of a Latina single mother, worked at McDonald's and sold plasma as a teenager, and later watched the family lose its home in the Great Recession. He says he has been an economist for the Army Corps of Engineers, a lawyer, and a state representative from Adams County. He says he would expand tax credits for working parents, close corporate tax loopholes, and bring down the cost of drugs, insurance premiums, and energy bills. He says he will protect Social Security and Medicare from benefit cuts and a higher retirement age, and cap insulin at $35 a month. He says his campaign takes no corporate PAC money, and that he would ban members of Congress from trading stocks and push to undo Citizens United.
Attorney General · District of Columbia · Republican

Attorney He says he has practiced law for decades and has spent his life in this community. He says he is running to bring that legal experience to the Office of the Attorney General. He says the office should put public safety first, enforce the law fairly, and stand with residents rather than special interests. He says it should protect victims, defend consumers, and fight corruption. He says it should work with the Metropolitan Police Department, the mayor, and the D.C. Council to make neighborhoods safer.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 9th District. Her campaign says she still lives in the small Toledo house where she grew up in a UAW family, and that she entered public service after watching factories close. It says she will back an idea from either party if she thinks it helps northwest Ohio. She says she would oppose foreign bailouts and wars she argues put Wall Street ahead of northwest Ohio, and make data-center companies pay for the power and water they use. She says she would take on corporate buyers of houses and expand the supply of affordable homes. She says she would fully fund Medicare and Medicaid, restore Affordable Care Act tax credits, and lower prescription prices and the cost of child care and long-term care.

State representative, 12th District, since 2021 · chairs Financial Institutions Chicago. Previously deputy chief of staff at the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity. She voted for the recent budgets Democrats credit with paying down the bill backlog and lifting the state’s credit. She calls the budget a moral document and says the job is to make every dollar traceable. A public “budget to bill” tool: from the line in the budget to the day the check goes out. Connect the office’s software to other agencies, use predictive models to catch missed federal matches and fraud, and send staff to help small vendors and local governments with late audits. Keep withholding pay from contractors who violate the Prevailing Wage Act. Change the Vendor Payment Program so finance firms cannot cherry-pick the receivables of larger vendors. Rebuild the rainy-day fund and make pension payments.

U.S. representative for Florida's 27th District Her campaign says she was born in Miami's Little Havana to Cuban parents who fled after Fidel Castro took power. She graduated from the University of Miami and from Harvard, which she says she paid for herself, then anchored CNN en Español, covered the White House and wars in the Gulf and El Salvador, and interviewed Fidel Castro. She says she won five Emmy Awards and was elected to Congress in 2020. She says she has voted to lower taxes, backed small businesses, and worked to recover pandemic money lost to fraud. She says she is funding Everglades restoration, coastal flood protection, and cleaner water in Biscayne Bay. She says she opposes socialism and communism, has pushed sanctions on the governments of Cuba, Venezuela, and Nicaragua, and supports term limits.

Attorney and former city council member running for Congress in Ohio's 14th District. Maria Jukic says she is a licensed attorney, a former Euclid councilwoman, and the child of immigrants from a union family, and that she worked in health care for 24 years. She says she is running for people in the political middle who are doing everything right and still falling behind. She says she will defend the Constitution and the rule of law, and that she is looking for practical answers to a health system in which many people lack insurance or carry medical debt. She says she will stand up for workers and regular people and look for common ground instead of sorting the country into two extremes.

Louisville trauma nurse and small-business owner running for Congress. Born in Cuba, she says she arrived in the United States at 21 after an 11-year asylum process, became a citizen, built a small business, and later earned a nursing degree as a single mother of two. She says she is running to defend freedoms she once lived without. She says she believes in free enterprise, safe communities, legal immigration, and constitutional rights. Her campaign lists defending capitalism, a safer Louisville, lower taxes, and protecting the unborn among her priorities. She also lists protecting women's sports.

Doctor, Army veteran, and U.S. representative running for re-election. She says she is the fourth of eight children, left home at 16 for community college, and enlisted in the Army at 18, rising from private to lieutenant colonel over 24 years. She later practiced medicine in Ottumwa, served in the Iowa Senate, and was elected to Congress in 2020. She says she is running for re-election because Iowans deserve someone who will keep fighting for them and for Iowa values. On her 2026 tour she says she is fighting for lower health-care costs, lower taxes, and common sense.

U.S. representative and auto-shop owner from southwest Washington. She describes herself as a fifth-generation Washingtonian, a pro-choice mother, and a trades small-business owner who built a house by hand and brought her child to work because day care was too expensive. She says she will oppose a national abortion ban and protect the freedom to see a doctor. She wants local police and firefighters paid enough to stay, and she is pushing a right to repair so farmers and customers are not forced back to the manufacturer. She says the campaign takes no corporate PAC money and is working to lower housing, child care, and health-care costs.

U.S. representative working on family costs, health care, and military families. She says she is a proud Army brat representing service members, veterans, and military families, and that her time in Congress has centered on costs, jobs, and care. She says working people and small businesses need lower costs, more jobs, and an economy put back on track. She wants health care people can afford, Medicare protected, and more renewable energy. She says she has led bipartisan work on food insecurity and housing for military families in a district she describes as full of service members and veterans.

U.S. representative for Florida's 26th District His campaign says he was born and raised in Florida, spent 14 years in the Florida Legislature, and was the youngest person elected to the Florida Senate, at 31. He is in his eleventh term in the U.S. House, vice chair of the Appropriations Committee, and founder of the bipartisan Everglades Caucus. He says he would end the tax on tips and overtime and make working-family tax cuts permanent. He says he would detain and remove people here illegally who have committed crimes, and crack down on fentanyl trafficking. He says he would continue Everglades restoration and fund school-violence prevention and parental rights in education.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

U.S. representative campaigning as a conservative voice for rural Missouri. He tells voters he spent more than 23 years as a local television anchor before taking that platform to Congress. He says he is fully opposed to abortion and will defend what he calls a right to life for the unborn. He wants federal spending, waste, and fraud cut back in order to slow the national debt. He says he will defend the Second Amendment for law-abiding owners and will oppose efforts to reduce police funding.

Colorado state senator and Republican nominee for U.S. Senate. Mark Baisley says he is an aerospace engineer who leads a Colorado software company and has served in the state House and the state Senate. He says he is the Republican nominee for the U.S. Senate in 2026. He says that in the legislature he worked on jobs, education, and essential services while limiting government intrusion into private life. He says he has defended water rights, protected the energy industry, and opposed reckless spending and government overreach. He says he will take that approach to Washington, with an emphasis on liberty and Colorado families.

U.S. representative running for another term. Mark DeSaulnier's campaign says he drove trucks, waited tables, and ran Bay Area restaurants before serving on the Concord council, as county supervisor, and in the Legislature. It says he has represented an East Bay House district, sits on Transportation and Infrastructure, and is the top Democrat on Ethics. He says workers need a voice as artificial intelligence changes jobs, and he points to proposals on layoffs, CEO pay, and the right to organize. He says housing, transit, and wages have to be tackled together so families are not pushed out of the Bay Area, and he highlights clean-air rules and a national electric-vehicle charging program. He says he would protect cancer-research funding, codify abortion and contraception access, and pursue immigration enforcement that does not separate families.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.
Secretary of State · South Carolina · Republican

Candidate for South Carolina secretary of state. His campaign says South Carolina businesses are growing and that the secretary of state's office has made filings easier. He asks voters to share that record as the campaign continues. He says Business One Stop has made it easier for businesses to expand in the state. He credits the High Growth Small Business Job Creation Act with drawing angel investment into early-stage, high-growth companies. He says oversight of charities is part of why the state ranks in the top five nationally for charitable giving.
District 8 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Republican

Pastor and U.S. representative for North Carolina's 8th District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Winston-Salem, the youngest of five children, and is a husband, father, and pastor. He says he is running again as an America First voice for the district. He says he believes in the sanctity of life from conception to natural death and in what he calls traditional family values. He says he would fortify the border, enforce immigration law, and keep a strong military that honors veterans. He says parents, not Washington, should choose public, private, charter, or home schools, and he wants to cut spending that he says drove inflation.

Retired Pinal County sheriff running for Congress in Arizona's 5th District. His campaign says he is not a career politician. It says he spent eight years as sheriff protecting Arizona communities, confronting cartels, and fighting human trafficking. He says he will secure the border, stop the cartels, and restore order to immigration while protecting legal immigration and commerce. He says he will defend the Constitution, support law enforcement, and stand with families and small businesses. He says he wants lower costs, protection for taxpayers, and stronger American jobs.

Small-business owner and U.S. representative from southern Indiana. A lifelong Hoosier from the Jasper area, he says he and his wife Kim have been married 40 years and have four children. He says less government creates more jobs, and that in the state legislature he fought for economic growth, individual liberties, and constitutional values. He says voters should know he is a Hoosier businessman and a Christian who will stand up to what he calls the woke mob in Washington. He says he is a pro-Trump conservative and will keep fighting for the values he learned growing up in Jasper. He says faith, family, and hard work are what make communities strong, and that he wants those communities more prosperous.

Educator and former council member running for Congress. Mark Nair's campaign says he is a husband, father, inventor, and former Amarillo city council member who has lived in the district for more than 30 years. It says he taught at Amarillo College, led innovation at a local employer, and holds patents. He says tariffs should be set by Congress rather than a president, and that he wants wages people can live on. He says government should stop using artificial intelligence for facial recognition and social-media surveillance until privacy rules exist, and that workers should know when AI affects their jobs. He says health care should put people ahead of insurers and corporate profits.

U.S. representative and former Wisconsin state legislator. He says his politics started in blue-collar Kenosha, where at age eight he delivered literature for his father, a city alderman. He took 14 years in the Assembly to Congress in 2013 and co-chairs the LGBT Equality Caucus and the Labor Caucus. He says he uses private-sector and public-sector experience to promote job growth and support families in south-central Wisconsin. He is chair emeritus of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and describes himself as a progressive leader. A campaign news note says he stopped taking corporate PAC money for his reelection.

U.S. representative and former teacher running for another term. Mark Takano's campaign says he was born and raised in Riverside, taught high school, and served on a community-college board before Congress. It says his parents and grandparents were sent to Japanese American incarceration camps during World War II, and that in 2012 he became the first openly gay person of color elected to Congress. He says that as a teacher and trustee he worked on public education and job training for adults. His campaign says he is the ranking Democrat on the House Veterans' Affairs Committee and also serves on Education and the Workforce.

Businessman and former state representative running for Congress. His campaign says he is a Christian husband, father, and grandfather who spent more than 30 years building insurance and construction businesses in Tulsa. It says that in the state House he helped pass a large tax cut, immigration enforcement, and a homeowner bill of rights. He says he would lower costs for working families by cutting inflationary spending, red tape, and energy and regulatory costs, and by restoring fiscal discipline. He says every nation has a right to secure its borders, enforce its laws, and put its citizens first. He says he is running to help build an economy that works for the people who fund it and to bring good jobs back.

Former major-league player running for Congress. Mark Teixeira's campaign says he is a Christian husband and father and a former All-Star whose father was a Navy veteran and whose mother was a teacher. It says five seasons with the Texas Rangers tied him to the state, and that he moved back in 2021. He says he would secure the border, deport people here illegally, and go after cartels. He says he would cut federal spending, expand oil, gas, and nuclear production, and defend parental rights, the Second Amendment, and the unborn.

U.S. senator whose campaign says he helped write the Affordable Care Act and a bipartisan infrastructure law. His campaign says he was the first in his family to finish college, that his first two businesses failed, and that a later company succeeded. It says he is the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee and has worked with both parties on bills signed into law. He wants more housing through rehabilitation and faster permits, and an easier path to a first mortgage, and he says lower health costs depend on a basic standard of care for every American. He says companies that profit from artificial intelligence should help prepare workers and pay for the energy that technology will demand. He supports an assault-weapons ban and background checks, and he says Virginia voters should be able to put abortion access, marriage equality, and restoration of voting rights into the state constitution.

Farmer, business owner, and U.S. representative from Howe, Indiana. A fourth-generation farmer, he says he started a beef cattle operation at 16, served in the Indiana House and Senate, and was elected to Congress in 2010. He and his wife Christy still farm at Schonbrook Farm and own businesses including a farm-to-fork restaurant. He says Washington's debt and spending, which he puts at $37 trillion, are the biggest threat to the American dream, and that waste should be cut without raising taxes. He says a repaired tax system should let workers keep more of what they earn, and that Social Security and Medicare can be preserved alongside entitlement reforms that reduce the debt. He says he wants to finish a border wall and strengthen national security.

Attorney and former prosecutor running for Congress. Marni von Wilpert's campaign says she is a workers'-rights attorney from the Obama years and a former prosecutor. It says she has gone after wage theft, opioid companies, and chemical polluters, launched first-time homebuyer grants, and defended abortion rights. She says she is running to lower costs for working families and to clean up corruption in Washington. She says that as the daughter of an immigrant Army veteran she is fighting ICE tactics she calls unconstitutional, including masked agents. She says she wants a secure border and a path to citizenship for long-term residents and Dreamers.

Iowa Colony council member running for Congress. Marquette Greene-Scott's campaign says she is mayor pro tem of Iowa Colony, the youngest of five children of a Vietnam veteran, and the mother of an adult daughter. It says she moved to Texas in 2010 as a single mother and recently married. She says she is running because Congress is broken and she will judge issues by what is best for the district rather than by party. She says her focus is creating jobs, improving infrastructure, and protecting essential rights.
Candidate for the U.S. Senate. Her campaign site calls her a champion for Tennessee and says the campaign is powered by ordinary people. No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Candidate for governor of Tennessee. Her campaign says that, as a member of the Tennessee Senate, she led the fight against a state income tax. She is running for governor on a promise to keep that low-tax direction and draw more jobs to the state. She says she will keep taxes and prices low and cut spending and regulation she calls unnecessary so more companies move to Tennessee. She says she will help Tennessee-grown small businesses expand at home while the state recruits outside employers. She says she will work with businesses on workforce gaps, including training, and commit to filling them.

Minister running for Congress. Martha Fierro's campaign says she is a Houston-raised Latina, a first-generation college graduate of the University of Houston, and director of a prayer network that works with churches. It says she has been married for more than 30 years, has five children, and started as a health-care worker at 19. She says health care should get more affordable through competition and patient choice rather than government mandates, and she supports school choice and parental rights. She says she would cut federal spending, back Texas oil and gas, and support Border Patrol against illegal crossings and trafficking.
District 3 · U.S. House · New Mexico · Republican

State representative running for Congress. Martin Zamora's campaign says he was born on a farm near Clovis, has worked in agriculture, cattle, and other businesses, and has represented New Mexico House District 63 since 2019. It says he and his wife Debbie live in Clovis. He says he would defend private property and water rights and cut federal rules he says burden farmers and ranchers. He says he would lower taxes, cut red tape, and support small businesses as the source of jobs. He says he would stand with law enforcement against fentanyl and other drug trafficking, and would secure the southern border.
District 1 · U.S. House · South Dakota · Republican

Former attorney general running for Congress in South Dakota. His campaign says he kept South Dakota safe as attorney general and as U.S. attorney, and that he is running to take that record to Congress. It says his father, a lawyer and former Meade County state's attorney, administered the oath when Marty became attorney general. The campaign says the job in Congress is to keep South Dakota safe, and it points to three years as U.S. attorney and three elections as attorney general. The site highlights an A+ NRA rating and endorsements that include the NRA-PVF and South Dakota Right to Life.

Republican candidate for Nevada's 3rd District. His campaign says he earned a master of music in composition from USC, wrote commercial music and film scores, and later became audio director and composer at Bungie as the studio developed Halo. He says he is retired, has been married since 1977, and has two daughters and three grandsons. On the economy he says automation and AI are squeezing both blue-collar and white-collar work, and he wants investment in those tools paired with safeguards for American workers. He says securing the border is a federal duty, credits lower crossings to the current administration, and says the country should keep building border controls and target human and drug trafficking. On the debt he says higher deficits raise mortgage rates and inflation, and he wants spending sorted into what is critical, what can wait, and what can be cut so the budget can move toward balance.

Army National Guard chaplain and restructuring executive running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 6th District. Marty Young is a fourth-generation Pennsylvanian and West Point graduate who served as an infantry officer and now as a lieutenant colonel and Army National Guard chaplain. He says he has spent 25 years stabilizing companies in defense, aerospace, manufacturing, and technology. His platform focuses on making family life affordable, fixing health care, protecting public safety, strengthening energy security, and supporting the military. He says his Young Americans Plan would extend real coverage to children up to age 23 and to expectant mothers, and that he wants to create jobs, secure the border, and cut waste.

Evansville city councilor, small-business owner, and Army Reserve veteran running for Congress. She says she has lived in Indiana more than 30 years, returned to Evansville after military training to raise three daughters, and serves as an at-large city councilor and vice president of the council. She says she has owned a small business for more than 15 years and chairs the Enterprise Zone board. She says health care is a human right and that she would protect and expand Medicaid and Medicare and keep rural hospitals open. She says universal coverage, not tied to a job, would lower costs by focusing on prevention and let people change jobs or start businesses without losing doctors. She says every Hoosier deserves a decent place to live, food on the table, and a home they can keep livable.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 5th District. Mary Gay Scanlon's office says she joined the House after a 2018 special election. She worked as a lawyer for low-income clients, including as national pro bono counsel and at the Education Law Center, and she was president of her local school board. She and her husband Mark live in Swarthmore and have three adult children. Her office says her priorities are voting rights, access to justice, education, economic growth in the region, gun safety, women's rights, and ending hunger. She says her main goal is protecting and improving the lives of children, families, veterans, and seniors.

Candidate for U.S. Senate Mary Peltola says she grew up on the Kuskokwim fishing salmon and is running for Senate because she has seen government fail Alaskans. Her campaign says she backed oil and gas development, including approval of the Willow project, and wants energy costs brought down. She wants permitting reform and more refining of Alaska oil, including the Alaska LNG pipeline, so energy costs fall and jobs stay in the state. She says she will push to modernize aging grids, including the Railbelt, and restore federal tax credits for solar, wind, and hydropower. She says she will expand heating assistance so families are not left without heat when federal funding is delayed.

Candidate for Congress in Washington's 1st District. Her issues page lays out what she calls an America-first platform on jobs, security, spending, and elections. Her platform calls for bringing semiconductor, IT, AI, and cybersecurity work back to the United States and for restructuring H-1B visas so companies hire locally. She wants stronger border security, a review of security clearances, and an audit of the Pentagon and intelligence contracting. She supports voter ID and a midweek election holiday, and she says patients, including parents, should control medical decisions.

Candidate for Congress in Georgia's 2nd District. His campaign points to work in glazing, construction, software, and real estate, and he describes himself as a timber man. He says he is on a mission for God and country to fight corruption, waste, and the size of government. His local list includes fathers who show up, ending generational poverty, farmers, teachers, manufacturing, white-collar jobs, rural health care, timber, ports, and pharmacists. He also says he is working to save the Okefenokee Swamp and lists national priorities that include Social Security, Medicare, and the cost of living. He says he is going to Washington to fight what he calls a woke liberal agenda and to defend Christianity and conservative freedoms.

Former Lakeville mayor and state senator running for Congress. Matt Little's site says he was born and raised in Lakeville, served as mayor, state senator, and city councilor, and owns a law firm representing seniors and people with disabilities. He says he lives in New Market Township with his wife, Coco, and their daughter. He says he is fighting for Medicare for All, affordable child care, tax breaks for everyday Americans, and a tax on the ultrawealthy. He says he wants a moratorium on data centers, an end to Citizens United, and corporate PAC money out of politics. He says he will champion women's reproductive freedom and keep Minnesota a refuge for LGBTQ people.

Libertarian candidate for the U.S. Senate. His campaign says he grew up in a suburb south of Denver, worked in video game development, and bought a house in Idaho's Treasure Valley in 2020. He says he splits his time between his church, developing a video game, hiking in the Rockies, and work for the Libertarian Party of Idaho. He says the border should be closed except to people invited by citizen landowners who take financial responsibility for them, that uninvited immigrants should be deported, and that he would end birthright citizenship. He says he would repeal minimum-wage laws and the Affordable Care Act, end the Federal Reserve, and cut federal budgets rather than only slow their growth. He says no U.S. troops should be sent outside the country unless Congress declares war, that the government should send no money or weapons abroad, and that he would abolish the VA and pay veterans directly for care.

U.S. representative, West Point graduate, and Army helicopter pilot. His campaign says he is a decorated combat veteran who served 10 years on active duty, including as an air mission commander, and that he was a commissioner in Governor Bill Lee's administration. He says he lives Tennessee's values with his wife and daughter. He says he would cut red tape, bring manufacturing back, unleash American energy, and set rules for crypto and artificial intelligence that protect privacy. He says he would reform the VA so veterans get the care and benefits they earned, finish the border wall, and stop fentanyl trafficking. He says he would protect farmers from overregulation and foreign land purchases and expand rural health care.

Maine state auditor running for Congress. Matt Dunlap's site says he was born and raised on a farm near Bar Harbor, worked as a dishwasher, bartender, and fur trapper, and later led the Sportsman's Alliance of Maine. He says that as state auditor he works to cut waste and prevent fraud, and that he and his wife, Michelle Dunphy, live in Old Town. He says he will fight blanket tariffs and the war in Iran, which he says have raised gas and grocery prices, and he supports universal child care, good-paying jobs, and more affordable housing. He says he will protect Medicare, Social Security, and Medicaid, reverse Medicaid cuts he says are hurting rural hospitals, and support Medicare for All. He says he is fully pro-labor, supports the PRO Act, and will defend a woman's right to make her own reproductive decisions.

Planner and Democratic nominee for Florida's 17th District His campaign says he was born in South Bend, Indiana, into a family of eleven, and started working in high school as a farmhand, janitor, messenger, and store clerk. He earned a bachelor's degree in political science and Spanish from Catholic University and a master's in public administration from Indiana University, then spent two years in the Peace Corps and 27 years with the UN Food and Agriculture Organization. He says he has lived in the district since the 1990s. He says he would ease housing costs with workforce housing for teachers, first responders, and families, and take on Florida's property-insurance crisis. He says he would make health-care and prescription prices more transparent without taking away consumer choices. He says he would modernize border security and create a background-checked path to legal status for people already working in Florida's farms and small businesses.

Governor of Massachusetts, running for re-election with Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll. Maura Healey's campaign says she and Kim Driscoll were elected in 2022 as the first all-women executive team in the nation's history and are running again to keep lowering costs. Her campaign says the first term ended renter's fees, capped health-care deductibles and co-pays, opposed utility rate increases, cut taxes, and protected SNAP from federal cuts. It also points to work on the MBTA, free school meals, free community college, and veterans' homes. For a second term she says she will defend health care and abortion rights, access to vaccines, research, jobs, and lower costs, and stand up to Donald Trump.

Retired Army officer and former VA health worker running for Congress. She says she served 26 years in the Army, from enlisted military police to lieutenant colonel, received the General Douglas MacArthur Leadership Award, and later worked in health care at the Atlanta VA. Born in Massachusetts, she says she has lived in Georgia for more than 30 years and is running again after getting no help from her member of Congress for veteran patients. She supports a higher minimum wage, labor rights, affordable housing, Social Security that keeps up with inflation, and student-loan relief, and she says she would vote against funding a war with Iran. She backs the Agricultural Right to Repair Act, farm safety nets, prescription-drug caps, restored Medicare subsidies, and easier VA care, including telehealth for rural veterans. She also calls for stronger border enforcement alongside faster legal immigration, legal protections for LGBTQIA+ and BIPOC Americans, and infrastructure to handle storms, floods, and heat.

Former Pelham City Council president running for Congress The campaign says Maurice Mercer graduated from Troy University, works as an account executive, and served three terms on the Pelham City Council, including as president from 2020 to 2025. It says he was the council's first African American member and is running to focus on costs, health care, and civility. He says he will push to lower grocery, utility, and health costs and help working families keep more of what they earn. He supports wider access to affordable care, rural providers, mental health services, and clearer prescription prices. He supports secure borders and a path to legal status for people who have lived here, worked, and paid taxes, with enforcement aimed first at people who threaten public safety.

Republican nominee for Indiana secretary of state. Max Engling says he worked through college in construction, earned a degree at IUPUI, and later a master's in national defense and strategic planning at the U.S. Naval War College. He describes work on the U.S. House Administration Committee, in House leadership, at an Indiana seed company, and most recently on the staff of U.S. Senator Jim Banks. He says he will work so that only eligible citizens vote in Indiana and will advocate closed primaries. He wants business filings screened for fraud, including shell companies, and he wants regulations on small businesses cut back. He proposes a public portal where people can report possible election problems.
District 4 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Republican

Candidate for Congress in North Carolina's 4th District. His campaign describes him as a constitutionalist and calls him an anti-socialism warrior. He says he is not a traditional Republican and does not see people by race. He says his policies are meant to expand opportunity, strengthen families, and increase prosperity for every American. He says he is running to represent all of the people, not some of them.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 7th District. Max Miller is in his second term and says he grew up in northeast Ohio, served six years in the Marine Corps Reserve, and spent four years in the White House as director of presidential advance and a senior advisor to Donald Trump. His father owns a cap manufacturing company in Cleveland. He says he has voted to make tax cuts permanent and to end taxes on tips and overtime, and that workforce training should not require a four-year degree. He also says he will fund law enforcement, keep the southern border secure, expand American energy, and invest in roads, bridges, rail, and broadband.

Attorney from Hazel Crest DePaul and Valparaiso Law. Has been a Grande Prairie library trustee and an adjunct political-science instructor at South Suburban College. He dropped a long-shot race for governor and won more than 60,000 write-in votes in March to make this ballot. He had under $5,000 on hand on October 1, against Frerichs’s roughly $1.6 million. “Illinois first.” He says state money should not be invested with foreign governments, and that he would take a lower return to keep investments here. He did not name a Frerichs investment he considers political. Use the office as “whistleblower-in-chief” on waste and fraud, including pressure on the legislature. Much of that is outside the treasurer’s formal powers. His campaign also lists a public dashboard of state funds and a stronger Bright Start and Bright Directions.

U.S. representative and physician for Oregon's 3rd District, seeking another term. Her campaign says she grew up in the Pacific Northwest, worked at a grocery store as a union member, and became the first in her family to finish college and medical school at the University of Washington. It says she practiced at Kaiser Permanente, served in the Oregon House, and now represents the 3rd District. She says she is working to protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, and she lists universal, affordable health care, addiction and mental-health treatment, and reproductive care among her priorities. She also names economic opportunity, climate and environmental protection, housing, gun-violence prevention, and schools. Her issues page includes government corruption, immigration, LGBTQ protections, and safeguarding democracy.

U.S. representative for California's 43rd District. Her office says she has served in Congress since 1991, after 14 years in the California Assembly, and was the first woman and first African American to chair the House Financial Services Committee. She was born in St. Louis, the fifth of 13 children, and earned a bachelor's degree from California State University, Los Angeles. Her office says expanding health care is a priority, including the Minority AIDS Initiative and services for diabetes, cancer, and Alzheimer's disease. Her office says she has worked to keep families in their homes and wrote the Neighborhood Stabilization Program to fight foreclosures and blight. Her office says she works to limit the harm of expanding Los Angeles International Airport and to preserve the Ballona wetlands.

U.S. representative running for another term. Maxwell Frost's campaign says he was adopted after his mother could not afford another child, saw police abuse and gun violence growing up, and organized with the ACLU, including Florida's voting-rights campaign. He says that as the first Generation Z member of Congress he is fighting to end gun violence, win Medicare for All, change the criminal justice system, and address the climate crisis. He says he pressed to end the Hyde Amendment and organized to restore voting rights to Floridians with past felony convictions.

Republican candidate for attorney general. He says he is a seventh-generation Texan, an attorney, president of an independent oil company, and a rancher who represents Senate District 11 after two terms in the Texas House. He says he rejects the state pension and health coverage and gives his state salary to local charities. He says as attorney general he will sue sanctuary cities, enforce federal border and deportation orders, and fight human trafficking. He says he will defend laws protecting unborn children, keep males out of women's sports and private spaces, and enforce voter-identification and citizenship rules for voting. He says he will go after waste, fraud, and abuse, enforce the open-records law, and protect oil and gas jobs from activists he calls far left.

Mechanic and community advocate from Bowling Green running for Congress. Born and raised in Bowling Green, she says she earned an automotive technology degree at Southcentral Kentucky Community and Technical College and works as a mechanic. She says she is also a caregiver and activist running because the district needs someone who knows what it is to struggle. She says one job should support a family, workers need a living wage, and health care should be universal so illness does not cause bankruptcy. She says she would protect reproductive freedom, support universal pre-K and affordable child care, and expand VA care, mental-health services, and housing for veterans. She says she signed a term-limits pledge and wants independent mechanics to have access to vehicle diagnostics that manufacturers now lock behind paywalls.
District 1 · U.S. House · New Mexico · Democratic

U.S. representative running for another term. Melanie Stansbury's campaign says she grew up in a working family in Albuquerque, served in the New Mexico House from 2019 to 2021, and has been in Congress since 2021. It says her work has focused on land, water, jobs, and hunger. She says she would expand the economy, support local businesses, and raise the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour. She says health care is a human right and that she supports Medicare for All, lower out-of-pocket costs, and protection for pre-existing conditions. She says she would keep working on climate, renewable energy, water security, and public lands.

Democratic socialist running for U.S. House in Colorado's 1st District. Melat Kiros says she was born in Addis Ababa and that her family moved to Denver after her father was selected in the diversity-visa lottery. She says she earned a law degree, lost a New York law job after refusing to take down an article defending students who protested Israel, and is now a doctoral student and a barista. She says she rejects corporate PAC money and will stand for Medicare for All, a housing-first approach to homelessness, universal child care, and an arms embargo. She says medical bills should not bankrupt people, and that she would abolish ICE and replace it with an immigration system aimed at public safety. She says universal child care would keep parents from having to choose between work and paying the equivalent of a second rent.

Former Dublin mayor and BART director running for Congress. Melissa Hernandez's campaign says she is the daughter of migrant farmworkers, a working mother who paid her way through college, and the first Latina mayor of Dublin. It says she also serves on the BART board and as a county health-care director. She says her first priority is lowering housing, health-care, and child-care costs, protecting Social Security and Medicare, and growing small businesses without raising taxes. She says public safety should support police and firefighters and also demand that enforcement work fairly. She says she would lower drug prices, restore insurance subsidies, and protect reproductive care.

Real estate broker running for Congress. Melissa McDonough's campaign says she has lived in Harris County for nearly 30 years and is a mother, businesswoman, and community organizer. It says she has worked as a realtor and brokerage owner and has helped run Harris County elections. She says she would protect Social Security, fund public schools, make tuition more affordable, and support renewable energy and flood control. She says she supports responsible gun ownership, letting women make their own medical decisions, Medicare for All, and more effective border management.

Supply-chain director from northern Kentucky running for Congress. A lifelong northern Kentuckian from Villa Hills, she says she earned degrees at Northern Kentucky University and Thomas More while working, and has spent about 27 years in food manufacturing and supply chain. She and her husband Andy live in Erlanger and have two sons. She says she would protect and expand Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security, lower drug costs, and make treatment easier to find than a dealer. She says she takes no corporate or foreign PAC money and supports term limits, a ban on congressional stock trading, and an end to Citizens United. She says data centers should need community approval, and she wants the government out of reproductive health care and a right to repair farm and consumer equipment.
District 7 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Tenant organizer from Bushwick running for Congress in New York's 7th District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Bushwick and has spent more than 30 years as a community activist and tenant organizer, including work against illegitimate rent increases and predatory real-estate speculation. It says he experienced homelessness earlier in life and is running independent of party loyalty. He says public assistance should build independence, with apprenticeships aimed at higher-paying work and room for families to keep benefits while they advance. He says tenants should get the first chance to buy when a landlord decides to sell, so more renters can become homeowners. He also names free enterprise, breaking monopolies, and holding government accountable among his top priorities.

Army veteran and attorney running for Congress. Micah Jones's site says he is a U.S. Army veteran, an attorney, and a husband and father of two who used the GI Bill to attend Northeastern University School of Law and later practiced securities enforcement in Boston. He says his family lives in Essex on the North Shore. He says accountability means officials are answerable to the people, and he backs conflict-of-interest rules, congressional term limits, and Congress reclaiming its constitutional duties. He says energy, grocery, housing, and child-care costs are shrinking opportunity, and he pledges work on energy reliability, faster permitting, and tax relief tied to child care and the state and local tax deduction. He says security should include support for service members, veterans, and first responders, a lawful and humane immigration system, and a technological edge in artificial intelligence.
District 12 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

State assemblymember running for Congress in New York's 12th District. His campaign says he is a lifelong Upper West Sider now in the Assembly, after serving as policy director for Governor Hochul, chief of staff at the attorney general's office, and an aide to Representative Jerry Nadler. It says that work included gun laws, abortion access, a higher minimum wage, and housing supply. He says Democrats should use every available lever against what he calls Trumpism and also spell out a positive agenda on affordability, health care, corruption, and climate. His platform also covers protecting immigrants and civil rights, reproductive freedom, public schools, and safeguards on big technology companies and artificial intelligence.

Medical director running for governor Michael Addison's campaign calls him a medical director who says he has cared for patients in South Carolina, and a certified inspector and property-damage analyst. It also describes him as a community organizer working on foreclosure prevention, job training, and help for people without housing. He says the state needs a governor who combines health-care knowledge with environmental accountability. He says prosperity has to start with people who are most vulnerable, including help with jobs and housing distress.

Construction worker and podcast producer running for Congress in Wisconsin's 7th District. His campaign says he was raised from Vilas County to Wausau, paid his way through a mathematics degree at UW-Madison with construction work, and married his high-school best friend at 22. It says his grandfather fled communist Cuba and that he later produced The Dan Bongino Show. He says he would cut spending and red tape so young families can buy homes, ease rules on farms, and back school choice and homeschooling. He says he is fully opposed to abortion and assisted suicide, would ban members of Congress from trading stocks, and would defend the Second Amendment, including constitutional carry. He says immigration policy, including H-1B visas, should serve American workers, and that he would return power to the states and stop spending he calls wasteful foreign aid.

District attorney running for Colorado attorney general. Michael Allen says he is the elected district attorney for El Paso and Teller counties, a former Navy aviation electronics technician, and a husband and father. He says he has worked as a prosecutor since a law-school internship in 2004. He says he will put victims first, use the statewide grand jury on crimes that cross county lines, and work with sheriffs and police across the state, including rural departments. He says he will review the attorney general's spending, cut waste, and treat crime as a driver of insurance and business costs. He says he will investigate public corruption without regard to party and will defend Colorado's water rights in disputes with other states.

Independent candidate for U.S. Senate Michael Bahry's campaign says he is a native Rhode Islander who has worked as a laborer, carpenter, construction executive, and business owner. It says he founded a Providence nonprofit in 2014 and later earned two master's degrees from Providence College. His campaign videos argue that Congress needs term limits and regular turnover. Other videos call the war in Gaza a tragedy and argue for peace rather than more bombing in Gaza and in the Russia-Ukraine war.

U.S. representative for Washington's 5th District. He says his first year in Congress coincided with fewer border crossings, less crime, lower taxes, and protection for the Lower Snake River dams. He says he is running so those policies stay in place. He describes the job as delivering results for families and for eastern Washington's regional interests.

Army National Guard captain running for Congress in Michigan's 10th District. His campaign says he is a third-generation Michigander, a Michigan State ROTC graduate, and a Bronze Star recipient who served with the 82nd and 101st Airborne Divisions, including the southern border and Iraq. It says his father is Oakland County Sheriff Mike Bouchard and his grandfather worked at General Motors. He says he would bring manufacturing jobs back to Michigan and cut red tape on small businesses. He says he would finish the border wall, restore Remain in Mexico, end catch-and-release, and stop fentanyl smuggling. He says schools should return to reading, writing, math, and science, and he backs a Parents' Bill of Rights.

Democratic nominee for Mississippi's 3rd District. His campaign says he is a farmer and entrepreneur who raises sheep, pigs, and cows in Shubuta, and that he earned an MBA from Felician University. He describes the race as a push for public investment that strengthens rural economies. He says simply raising taxes or cutting spending is not enough, and he wants federal investment in factories, farms, infrastructure, and a broader safety net so more people can take part in the economy. On health care he wants lower out-of-pocket costs and premiums, more trained medical workers, and modern facilities so people can age with access to care. He wants to expand USDA homebuilding, help small farms with loans, equipment, and new markets, and put federal money into a more resilient electric grid.

U.S. representative running for another term. Michael Cloud's campaign says he is a husband and father elected in 2018 to represent the coastal 27th District. It says he is a Freedom Caucus member who describes his mission as Christian, conservative, America First values. He says the border needs a wall and a response to cartels and trafficking, and that cutting regulation and simplifying the tax code would help small businesses. He says federal spending is on a path to ruin and he has filed bills to improve cost estimates and to sunset federal agencies.

Retired public school teacher. His campaign says he is a native North Carolinian, a recently retired teacher, and a community activist who has led a prison ministry for more than twenty years. He says he is a veteran and that this campaign refuses corporate PAC money. He says he would try to overturn Citizens United, end gerrymandering, and stop what he calls voter suppression. He says he wants a Green New Deal for the state, with renewable energy, union jobs, and accountability for corporate polluters. He says he prefers diplomacy to war and would reduce military spending in favor of schools, hospitals, and communities.

Louisiana state representative and business owner running for Congress. A lifelong northeast Louisiana resident and University of Louisiana at Monroe graduate, he says he chairs the House Republican delegation and works as a licensed contractor and commercial real-estate investor. He and his wife Christie, an architect, live in Monroe with two daughters. He says insurance premiums should fall if Washington lowers inflation, expands domestic energy, and drops federal rules that raise the cost of rebuilding after storms. He says grocery prices rose because of federal spending, and that cheaper fuel and fewer rules on farmers, truckers, and stores would bring checkout prices down. He says he would expand oil and gas production, support LNG exports, protect Louisiana refineries, and speed permits for energy projects.

Former Huntington Beach city attorney running for attorney general. Michael Gates says that as Huntington Beach city attorney he started a local criminal prosecution program aimed at quality-of-life crimes. He says public safety would be his first priority as attorney general. He says he will make statewide enforcement of Proposition 36 his top task and will prioritize prosecution of violent and repeat offenders. He says cities and counties, not the state, should control zoning and housing decisions, and that he will defend that local authority. He says he will investigate fraud in state programs and sue to recover public money.

Surgeon running for Congress The campaign says Dr. Mike Goldstein put himself through medical school, became a surgeon, and spent more than 30 years making decisions in the operating room. He says he is running to bring that same accountability to Congress. He says health care is expensive because regulation has reduced competition, not because medicine itself is costly. He argues that insurers answer to shareholders and that pharmacy middlemen take profit before drugs reach patients. He says the FDA has slowed access to treatments and that the Right to Try law has helped very few patients.

U.S. representative for Mississippi's 3rd District. Michael Guest's office says he is in his fourth term and previously was district attorney for Madison and Rankin Counties. He chairs the Border Security and Enforcement Subcommittee of the Homeland Security Committee. He says he believes in limited government, lower taxes, fewer regulations, the right to life of the unborn, a strong national defense, and Second Amendment rights. He says he works to secure the border and has opposed efforts to defund the police.
Secretary of State · North Dakota · Republican

Secretary of state of North Dakota. His campaign says he was elected the state's 15th secretary of state in 2022, after six years as a state representative and work as a fifth-generation farmer at Howe Seed Farms in Casselton. He is running for another term. He says he wants elections that stay secure and open to every eligible voter, including a citizenship check and a valid North Dakota ID for every form of voting. He says the state uses paper ballots, keeps ballot equipment off the internet, audits elections after the vote, and counts only ballots in by the close of polls. He says he will keep cutting red tape so North Dakota stays an easy place to start and grow a business.

Candidate for lieutenant governor Michael Kalagias is running for lieutenant governor. His campaign site argues Arkansas taxes too much while the state runs surpluses. He proposes cutting the state sales-tax rate from 6.5 percent to 5 percent and ending local sales tax on food, diapers, and feminine hygiene products. He wants the state standard deduction raised to the federal figure of $15,750 for each filer and dependent. He says the planned large prison should be canceled because he calls it a billion-dollar project the state does not need.
District 3 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Former state assemblyman running for Congress in New York's 3rd District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Farmingdale, the son of a nurse and a utility worker, and that he became a lawyer and then a state assemblyman. It says he won that seat by outworking a Democratic incumbent, including knocking on more than 20,000 doors. He says that in the Assembly he opposed policies he argues raised the cost of living and threatened Long Island's quality of life. He says he wants to help House Republicans secure the border, keep a higher state-and-local tax deduction, and cut what he calls waste, fraud, and abuse.

Engineer running for Congress. Michael Masuda's campaign says he grew up in Amador County, studied electrical engineering at Cal Poly, and helped develop military technology at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory. It says he later served as a foreign affairs officer at the State Department and lives in the 5th District with his wife and two young children. He says he would lower housing, health-care, and energy costs and send more federal money back to rural communities. He says wildfire work should include thinning, prescribed fire, home hardening, and faster disaster aid so insurance is more available. He says he would keep rural hospitals open, expand telehealth, protect Medicare and Medi-Cal, and support water and markets for farmers.
District 3 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Republican

Marine and Navy reservist running for Congress in New Jersey's 3rd District. His campaign says he is a husband, father, and veteran who served twice as a Marine and now serves in the Naval Reserve. He says he is not a politician and is running to put service ahead of self-interest. He says his first priority is affordability: cutting wasteful spending and lowering taxes so working families can keep more of what they earn. He says he wants people to feel safe at home and wants government held accountable. He says he fully supports a ban on stock trading by members of Congress and term limits.

Business leader and Army veteran running for governor. Mike Minogue's site describes him as a husband, father, combat veteran, and the business leader who took Abiomed from an idea to a global standard in cardiac care. He says a voter-backed audit of the Legislature is not being enforced and that the political establishment is wasting tax dollars and growing debt. He says taxes and regulation are pushing young people out and making it hard for seniors to stay, and he asks supporters to join a call to suspend the gas tax. He says the state needs entrepreneurs and manufacturing to stay and expand, and that the governor's basic job is public safety, including enforcement against fentanyl dealers.

Economist Michael Pakko says he spent more than 15 years as a research economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis and then was chief economist and state economic forecaster at the Arkansas Economic Development Institute at UA Little Rock. He says he has chaired the Libertarian Party of Arkansas for about a decade and was the party's 2024 nominee for treasurer. He says he will run elections as a professional operation, with accurate voter rolls, support for county clerks, published procedures, and counts the public can check. He says ballot access and rule-making should treat every candidate and party the same. He says election and business-filing data should be published in forms citizens and the press can use.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 6th District. Michael Rulli says he was born and raised in the Mahoning Valley and still runs Rulli Brothers Market, which his family started more than 100 years ago. He served as Leetonia school board president and in the Ohio Senate before winning a 2024 special election to Congress. He says that as school board president he led the district out of a financial crisis without raising taxes. He says that in the state Senate he brought funding back to communities and stood up for local values.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Incumbent since 2015 · former state senator · grew up in Gifford Won his first race by fewer than 10,000 votes. A win now would make him the longest-serving treasurer in state history. He describes the job as making money for the state, helping families save, and giving money back. Unclaimed property: he says the office returns about $1 million a day. This year that included $8.65 owed to Robert Prevost, now Pope Leo XIV, from an old PayPal account. Cites a Morningstar turnaround for Bright Start, and investment earnings above $1.4 billion in fiscal 2026. Local governments in the Illinois Funds earn interest he says they then do not have to raise in property taxes. Will keep Israel bonds. His test is return, safety, and diversification, and he says dropping them is a question for the legislature, not his office.

Massachusetts litigator running for attorney general. Michael Walsh's site says he was born and raised in Lynnfield, has practiced law in Massachusetts for 15 years, and earned his bachelor's degree and law degree at Suffolk University at unusually young ages. It says he has represented workers, homeowners, service members, and towns, and is currently litigating against the attorney general's office. He says he will enforce laws already on the books, including the legislative audit, with no selective enforcement. He opposes state zoning mandates that he says override local home rule and threaten funding. He says he will fight utility rate hikes, vet ballot questions for clarity and legality, and investigate fraud, waste, and abuse.

Republican candidate for U.S. Senate. His campaign says he has spent his career fighting for the country and for North Carolina's conservative values. He says he is running to take that fight to Washington and to put North Carolina first. He says he is running to fight for secure borders. He says he wants strong leadership and what he calls North Carolina values. He asks voters to stand with him and with President Trump.

Engineer and small-business owner running for Congress in Tennessee's 2nd District. Her campaign says she grew up doing barn chores on her family's horse farm, started a composting program in college, and later earned a doctorate in civil engineering while building a Knox County business. She says a year as a science-policy fellow in Congress convinced her the institution is not working for East Tennessee. She says gas, groceries, infrastructure, and rent are squeezing East Tennessee, and that both parties' insiders are waiting the problems out. She wants to limit corporate political spending, overturn Citizens United, ban congressional stock trading, and require independent redistricting commissions. She also calls for term limits, a lobbying ban after members leave office, and age limits for Congress and the presidency.

Former NFL sideline reporter and broadcaster. Her campaign says she is a four-time Sports Emmy winner who covered NFL games for NBC, including five Super Bowls, and left the sideline after Super Bowl LVI. She is running for the Senate on what she calls accountability and family-first leadership. She says she would cosponsor a bill to deport an immigrant convicted of fraud and would seek mandatory federal prison terms for fraud. She says she would push to withhold federal money from a state that will not put anti-fraud controls in place. She says Minnesota's criminal-justice experiment has failed and that she would stand with victims and law enforcement.

U.S. representative for Minnesota's 7th District. Michelle Fischbach's office says she has represented western Minnesota since 2021 and serves on Ways and Means and Rules. She was a Minnesota senator from 1996 to 2018, the first woman to serve as Senate president, and the state's 49th lieutenant governor. She and her husband Scott live on a hobby farm near Paynesville and have two children and seven grandchildren. She says she stands up for agriculture, Second Amendment rights, respect for law and order, and defending the unborn.

Attorney and Republican nominee for Florida's 14th District His campaign says he grew up in Brooklyn, graduated from Harvard Law during the Great Recession, and moved to Florida to practice law for individuals and small businesses. He served six years in the Florida House, then returned to his law practice and his family. He lives in southeast Hillsborough with his wife and two sons. He says he would expand clinics and telehealth so families do not have to travel an hour or take a day off work to see a doctor. He says he would cut spending that drives prices up, after backing what he calls the largest tax cut in Florida history and tax holidays on gas and everyday purchases. He says he would cut rules that block workers and small businesses, and require local approval before a data center is built so it does not raise energy bills.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 15th District. Mike Carey says he was born and raised in the 15th District, sworn in on November 4, 2021, and now serves on Ways and Means and House Administration as a deputy whip. His campaign describes him as a veteran. He says he is running to keep fighting for lower taxes, a stronger economy, secure borders, affordable energy, and safer communities. His campaign also lists protecting Social Security, supporting veterans and first responders, and reducing government spending.

Army veteran running for Congress. Mike Cargile's campaign says that as a young Army officer he swore an oath to defend the Constitution, and that he is running to fulfill it. It says the campaign takes no money from AIPAC, political parties, super PACs, corporations, or other special interests. He says the country should end endless wars, break up corporate monopolies, and become energy independent. He says fair and transparent elections are required to do that. He describes himself as pro-life, pro-jobs, and pro-police.

Trucking businessman running for the U.S. Senate. He says he used to haul freight and now wants to unseat Senator Jon Ossoff. His campaign describes him as someone who has worked for a living, created jobs, and passed what he calls America First legislation in Congress. He says Georgia needs a senator who has met tight schedules in the trucking industry, where he says you do not get paid if you do not deliver. He says working-class Americans are the backbone of the campaign and of the country, and he asks voters to join that fight.

Navy veteran and engineer running for Congress in Tennessee's 6th District. His campaign says he is a husband and father, a Navy veteran, an engineer, a former Tennessee state park ranger, and a former federal employee whose work connected to the State Department and NOAA. He says he earned degrees from Vanderbilt and Tennessee Tech. He organizes the campaign around affordability, accountability, and accessibility, including lower everyday costs and easier access to health care, voting, and veterans' services. He says he is not taking corporate PAC money and wants government to serve families rather than a powerful few. He says public officials, agencies, and corporations should be transparent and accountable.
District 11 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

Former teacher and paramedic running for Congress in New York's 11th District. His campaign says he is a fourth-generation Staten Islander and third-generation union member who has spent nearly 35 years in public service as a teacher, EMT, and paramedic. It says he treated injured firefighters at Ground Zero on September 11, 2001. He says Congress should act as a co-equal branch and put guardrails around civil and constitutional rights instead of leaving government to executive action alone. He says he would lower the tax burden on the working class, have billionaires pay a larger share, and stop what he calls the dismantling of the Education Department. He says he would also protect Social Security and Medicare and make groceries, gas, health care, and housing more affordable.

U.S. representative for Mississippi's 4th District. Mike Ezell's office says he is in his second term and is a Gulf Coast native who was Jackson County sheriff after more than forty years in law enforcement. He is a graduate of the University of Southern Mississippi, the Mississippi Law Enforcement Training Academy, and the FBI National Academy, and he chairs the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee. His office lists agriculture, conservative values, crime and public safety, immigration and border security, jobs and the economy, national security, transportation and infrastructure, and veterans among the issues he works on.

U.S. representative for Nebraska's 1st District The campaign says Mike Flood grew up in Norfolk, built Flood Communications from one radio station into a statewide group of radio and TV stations, and was the youngest speaker of the Nebraska Legislature. It says he was elected to Congress in a 2022 special election and chairs the Republican Main Street Caucus. He says he ran to lower taxes, secure the border, and cut wasteful spending, and that he backed a tax cut covering tips, overtime, and Social Security. The campaign says he voted for border-security funding and wrote a bipartisan bill aimed at making housing more affordable. He says he is running again to stretch paychecks further, restrain federal spending, and stand up to foreign adversaries, including China.

U.S. representative for Florida's 8th District His campaign says he is an educator and author who, with his wife Stephanie, raised three children in the district. He served in the Florida House and Senate, including as Senate president, and now chairs the House Space Committee and is a whip on the Financial Services Committee. He says he focuses on the space industry, the Indian River Lagoon, election integrity, a ban on congressional stock trading, and affordable housing. He says he would secure the border and fight inflation, higher taxes, and spending he calls reckless. State senator running for Congress in Michigan's 4th District. Former president of the University of Montana. Civics teacher and Democratic nominee for Florida's 3rd District His campaign says he teaches 7th-grade civics at Lincoln Middle School in Gainesville. Green Party candidate for secretary of state. He says he protected union jobs, delivered property-tax relief, and backed strong reproductive-health laws. He says he is running because working families are being squeezed while the wealthiest keep gaining more.

District 1 · U.S. House · North Dakota · Democratic

Democratic candidate for North Dakota's U.S. House seat. His campaign says he grew up in North Dakota, graduated from Velva High School, enlisted in the Navy, and graduated from the Naval Academy before choosing the Marine Corps. He served as a helicopter pilot and as an infantry officer in Iraq, retired as a major, and later taught science, worked in the Bakken, and counseled Job Corps students in Minot. He says Americans pay the world's highest health-care prices and that people should not have to choose between care and rent or food. He says he will protect Social Security and put North Dakota seniors first, and he opposes raising the retirement age. He says profitable corporations and the ultra-wealthy should pay a fair share, and that rural towns need support for public schools and farm markets, with Congress asserting its power over tariffs.

President of the Kansas Senate, running for governor. Ty Masterson's site says he was born and raised in Butler County, has been married to Marlo for 30 years, and has six children and seven grandchildren. He says he won local office in Andover more than twenty years ago and has stayed in public office since. He says that as Senate president he led a tax-cut package he calls the largest in Kansas history, and that he wants lower taxes, safer streets, and a government that answers to the people who pay for it. He proposes a Homeowners Bill of Rights aimed at property taxes and a stronger voice for taxpayers. He offers a Kansas Ratepayer Protection Pledge against higher costs he says outside interests would push onto families, farms, schools, hospitals, and small businesses.

Attorney and independent candidate for U.S. Senate. His campaign says he grew up in Rolling Fork, the son of a tractor driver, chopped cotton as a teenager, and was the first in his family to finish high school and attend college. He says he is running as an independent because he believes neither party is listening. He says health care is a right and that he supports the Medicare for All Act. He says he is not tied to either party or to lobbyists who profit from the current insurance system. He says his own father's untreated diabetes, and the loss of work and a vehicle that followed, is why the issue is personal.

Contractor and small-business owner running for Congress. Tyler Bass's site says he is a contractor, small-business owner, and former licensed life and health insurance agent who has worked since he was 10, including roofing, siding, and factory jobs. He says he started a business with a $250 paycheck after college. He says he will secure the border, support ICE, and remove people who are here illegally no matter how long they have been here, and cut H-1B loopholes so jobs go to Minnesotans. He says he will fight Washington's hand in local property taxes and will not vote to ban AR-15s, restrict magazine capacity, or add new hurdles for law-abiding gun owners. He says fraud that robbed children with autism and Minnesota taxpayers has to be confronted, and that his opponent has not spoken up about it.

Mattapoisett Select Board member running for Congress. Tyler Macallister's site says he is a lifelong Cape Codder who settled in Mattapoisett in 2001 with his wife, Cindy, and has served more than 20 years locally, including five terms on the Select Board. He describes himself as an advocate for sustainable fishing and the working waterfront. He says he will defend the fishing fleet with practical, science-based rules and oppose industrial wind farms in fishing grounds and data centers that drain the grid and water. He says he will take on mandates and federal spending that raise grocery, fuel, and housing costs, and he backs an all-of-the-above energy policy aimed at lower bills. He says he will back local police and child-safety standards, and protect the benefits veterans and seniors have earned.
